label: far from, not even
meaning_en: A particle meaning “far from X, not even X”: it dismisses the first item as out of the question and goes on to say that even something smaller or easier is not so either. It can also mean “on the contrary, far from X, the opposite”.
usage: It attaches to nouns as “은커녕” after a final consonant and “는커녕” after a vowel (“점심은커녕”), and it is written without a space. The clause after it is negative (“못”, “안”, “없다”), usually with “도” or “조차” on the lesser item. In the second sense the following clause states the opposite of what the noun would suggest (“성공은커녕 빚만 졌다”).

examples.ko: 너무 바빠서 점심은커녕 물 한 잔도 못 마셨어요.
examples.en: I was so busy that I couldn't drink even a glass of water, let alone have lunch.

examples.ko: 학생인 나는 자동차는커녕 자전거 한 대 살 돈도 없다.
examples.en: As a student I don't even have the money to buy a bicycle, let alone a car.

examples.ko: 지수는 된장찌개는커녕 라면도 제대로 못 끓인다.
examples.en: Jisu can't even boil instant noodles properly, let alone make doenjang stew.

examples.ko: 성공은커녕 빚만 잔뜩 지고 말았다.
examples.en: Far from succeeding, I ended up with nothing but a pile of debt.

examples.ko: 그 시간에는 버스는커녕 택시도 다니지 않았다.
examples.en: At that hour not even taxis ran, let alone buses.

compare.difference: “조차” picks out one extreme case; “은/는커녕” sets a big item against a smaller one, and both are negated.

pair.en: I could not even drink water.
I could not even drink water, let alone have lunch.

compare.difference: The two are close in meaning and are used in the same way.

pair.en: I couldn't even drink water, let alone have lunch.
I couldn't even drink water, let alone have lunch.

pitfalls.note: The clause that follows has to be negative.
pitfalls.en: I couldn't eat even porridge, let alone rice.

pitfalls.note: It is a particle, so it is written without a space.
pitfalls.en: I couldn't even drink water, let alone have lunch.

label: even if only a small thing
meaning_en: A particle meaning “even if it is only X, though it is modest”: the speaker accepts something small or short of what was wanted, and is glad of it.
usage: It attaches to nouns as “이나마” after a final consonant and “나마” after a vowel (“잠시나마”), and also to adverbs such as “늦게나마”. The noun names something modest (a short time, a small amount, a minor role), and the clause that follows is a positive result: thanks, relief or a modest achievement. It is used in speech and writing.

examples.ko: 짧은 시간이나마 가족과 함께 보낼 수 있어서 다행이다.
examples.en: I am glad I could spend even a short time with my family.

examples.ko: 단역이나마 그 영화에 출연할 수 있어서 기뻤다.
examples.en: I was happy to appear in that film, even if only in a bit part.

examples.ko: 늦게나마 진심으로 사과드립니다.
examples.en: I sincerely apologize, even if belatedly.

examples.ko: 작은 힘이나마 보태고 싶어서 기부를 했다.
examples.en: I made a donation because I wanted to add what little strength I could.

examples.ko: 잠시나마 걱정을 잊을 수 있었다.
examples.en: I was able to forget my worries, if only for a moment.

compare.difference: “이라도” offers something as the next best choice; “이나마” accepts something already in hand, though modest.

pair.en: I'm glad I could rest, if only briefly.
Rest, even if only briefly.

pitfalls.note: It presents something as modest, so it does not go with a large amount.
pitfalls.en: I donated, even if it was only a small sum.

pitfalls.note: After a vowel the particle is “나마”.
pitfalls.en: I could rest, if only briefly.

label: listing items: A and B and
meaning_en: A particle that strings nouns together as examples that belong in the same group: “X and Y and (so on)”. It is usually repeated after each item and is followed by a summing-up clause.
usage: It attaches to nouns as “이며” after a final consonant and “며” after a vowel (“채소며”). It is usually repeated (“A이며 B이며”), and the items are of the same kind. What follows sums them up: “모두”, “없는 게 없다”, “정리할 것이 많다”. It is used in speech and in prose.

examples.ko: 며칠 동안 폭우가 쏟아져 논이며 밭이며 모두 물에 잠겼다.
examples.en: Heavy rain poured for days, and rice paddies and fields alike were submerged.

examples.ko: 시장에는 과일이며 채소며 없는 게 없었다.
examples.en: At the market there was nothing you couldn't find, fruit and vegetables and more.

examples.ko: 방 안에는 책이며 옷이며 온갖 물건이 어질러져 있었다.
examples.en: In the room, books and clothes and all sorts of things were strewn about.

examples.ko: 이사를 하느라 가구며 짐이며 정리할 것이 산더미다.
examples.en: Because of the move, there's a mountain of furniture and luggage to sort out.

examples.ko: 그 가게는 값이며 품질이며 어느 하나 흠잡을 데가 없다.
examples.en: That shop has nothing to fault, neither the price nor the quality.

compare.difference: “하고” simply joins two items; “이며” repeats after each item to suggest a range of things of that kind.

pair.en: I bought a book and clothes.
I bought books and clothes and all sorts of things.

compare.difference: Both list examples of a kind. “이라든가” usually closes the list with “하는” plus a noun naming the category; “이며” is typically followed by a summing-up word such as “모두” or “온갖”.

pair.en: In the room, books and clothes were strewn about.

pair.ko: 책이라든가 옷이라든가 하는 것은 가져오지 마세요.
pair.en: Please don't bring things like books or clothes.

pitfalls.note: After a vowel it is “며”, not “이며”.
pitfalls.en: There was nothing you couldn't find, fruit and vegetables and more.

label: whichever, any one
meaning_en: A particle meaning that whichever one is chosen makes no difference: “be it X or Y, any, whatever”. With a question word it gives “anything, anyone, anywhere”.
usage: It attaches to nouns as “이든(지)” after a final consonant and “든(지)” after a vowel. Joined to a question word it gives “무엇이든”, “누구든”, “언제든지”, “어디든”. Used in pairs (“A든 B든”) it means “whether A or B”. The clause that follows says that the result is the same either way, often “괜찮다”, “좋다” or a general statement. “-든지” can be added with no change in meaning.

examples.ko: 무엇이든 좋으니 먹을 것 좀 주세요.
examples.en: Anything is fine, so please give me something to eat.

examples.ko: 언제든지 연락 주세요.
examples.en: Please contact me any time.

examples.ko: 커피든 차든 아무거나 좋아요.
examples.en: Coffee or tea, either is fine.

examples.ko: 누구든 이 문제를 풀 수 있다.
examples.en: Anyone can solve this problem.

examples.ko: 한국어 책이든 영어 책이든 읽을 만한 책이면 다 좋아요.
examples.en: Whether it's a Korean book or an English book, any book worth reading is fine.

compare.difference: “이나” offers a choice of one; “이든” says any choice is fine.

pair.en: Have coffee or tea.
Have anything, coffee or tea.

compare.difference: With a question word the two are close in meaning, though “이라도” can also mean “at least”.

pair.en: Anything is fine.
Anything at all is fine.

pitfalls.note: After a vowel the particle is “든”.
pitfalls.en: Coffee or tea, either is fine.

label: as for X, definition topic
meaning_en: A particle that picks out a noun as the topic to be defined or explained: “X is (by nature) Y, what we call X”. It is how one defines a term or states a general view.
usage: It attaches to nouns as “이란” after a final consonant and “란” after a vowel (“친구란”). The sentence that follows is a definition or a general statement, usually ending in “-ㄴ/는 것이다”, “-이다” or “-ㄴ/은 법이다”. It speaks of a kind of thing in general, not of one particular thing. It is common in essays and explanations and is a contraction of “이라는 것은”.

examples.ko: 사랑이란 서로를 이해하고 아끼는 마음이다.
examples.en: Love is understanding and cherishing each other.

examples.ko: 인생이란 한 권의 책과 같다.
examples.en: Life is like a book.

examples.ko: 친구란 어려울 때 곁에 있어 주는 사람이다.
examples.en: A friend is someone who stays by you in hard times.

examples.ko: 말이란 하기에 따라 칭찬도 되고 비난도 된다.
examples.en: Words can become praise or criticism depending on how they are said.

examples.ko: 교육이란 단순히 지식을 전달하는 일이 아니다.
examples.en: Education is not simply passing on knowledge.

compare.difference: “은/는” is the plain topic; “이란/란” sets the noun up as a thing to be defined.

pair.en: Love is a heart that cherishes each other.
Love is, by definition, a heart that cherishes each other.

compare.difference: “이라는” means “called, named” and goes before a noun; “이란” sets up a definition.

pair.en: The emotion called love is complicated.
Love is a complicated emotion.

pitfalls.note: After a vowel the particle is “란”.
pitfalls.wrong: 친구이란 어려울 때 곁에 있어 주는 사람이다.
pitfalls.right: 친구란 어려울 때 곁에 있어 주는 사람이다.
pitfalls.en: A friend is someone who stays by you in hard times.

pitfalls.note: It speaks of a kind of thing in general, not of one particular person.
pitfalls.right: 친구란 어려울 때 곁에 있어 주는 사람이다.
pitfalls.en: A friend is someone who stays by you in hard times.

topik_tip: In 읽기 passages “X란 Y이다” is the standard way to define a term, and the definition is usually the key point of the paragraph.

label: in every field, X or Y
meaning_en: A particle used in repeated pairs, “X이면 X, Y이면 Y”, to say that in every field or kind of thing named, the subject is outstanding or complete: “whether it's X or Y, nothing is lacking”.
usage: It attaches to a noun as “이면” after a final consonant and “면” after a vowel, and the same noun is repeated after it (“운동이면 운동”). Two or three such items are strung together, and the clause that follows is a sweeping claim, often a double negative (“못하는 게 없다”) or a word like “팔방미인”. It is spoken and written.

examples.ko: 승규는 운동이면 운동, 공부면 공부 못하는 게 없다.
examples.en: Seunggyu is good at everything, be it sports or studying.

examples.ko: 지수는 일이면 일, 살림이면 살림, 정말 팔방미인이다.
examples.en: Whether it is work or housekeeping, Jisu is truly a master of everything.

examples.ko: 이 가게는 맛이면 맛, 서비스면 서비스, 하나도 빠지는 게 없다.
examples.en: This shop lacks nothing, be it the taste or the service.

examples.ko: 우리 팀장님은 영어면 영어, 중국어면 중국어 다 능숙하세요.
examples.en: Our team leader is fluent in everything, English or Chinese.

examples.ko: 저 선수는 체력이면 체력, 기술이면 기술, 모든 면에서 뛰어나다.
examples.en: That player excels in every respect, be it stamina or skill.

compare.difference: “이며” just strings items together; “이면” repeats each noun and says that the subject is good at every one.

pair.ko: 운동이면 운동, 공부면 공부 다 잘한다.
pair.en: Be it sports or studies, they are good at all of it.
Sports and studies and the rest, they are good at all of it.

compare.difference: The ordinary “이면” means “if it is”; the repeated “X이면 X” means “in the field of X”.

pair.en: If tomorrow is a holiday, let's go hiking together.

pair.ko: 공부면 공부, 운동이면 운동 다 잘한다.
pair.en: Be it studying or sports, they are good at all of it.

pitfalls.note: The same noun is repeated, with each item kept together with its own “이면”.
pitfalls.wrong: 운동이면 공부, 노래면 춤 못하는 게 없다.
pitfalls.right: 운동이면 운동, 공부면 공부 못하는 게 없다.
pitfalls.en: There is nothing they can't do, be it sports or studying.

label: as for X, indeed (but)
meaning_en: A particle that puts weight on the noun before it: “as for X, of course, X at least, certainly”. It grants that the point holds, and the sentence usually goes on to give a contrast or a reservation.
usage: It attaches to nouns as “이야” after a final consonant and “야” after a vowel (“나야”, “지금이야”), and to some adverbs and endings. The main clause often has “-지만”, “-는데” or a similar concession. It is common in everyday speech. It is different from “이야말로”, which stresses “the very one”.

examples.ko: 글이야 잘 쓰지만 말은 서툴러요.
examples.en: I'm good at writing, yes, but I'm clumsy at speaking.

examples.ko: 나야 괜찮지만 다른 사람들이 걱정이야.
examples.en: I'm fine, but I'm worried about the others.

examples.ko: 지금이야 웃으며 말하지만 그때는 정말 힘들었다.
examples.en: I can talk about it laughing now, but back then it was really hard.

examples.ko: 돈이야 벌면 되지만 건강은 한번 잃으면 되찾기 어렵다.
examples.en: Money you can earn again, but health is hard to regain once lost.

examples.ko: 시험이야 어렵겠지만 열심히 준비하면 괜찮을 거예요.
examples.en: The exam will no doubt be hard, but if you prepare well you'll be fine.

compare.difference: “은/는” is the plain contrast topic; “이야” adds that the point is granted.

pair.en: I write well, but I'm clumsy at speaking.
Writing I do well, I admit, but I'm clumsy at speaking.

compare.difference: “이야말로” singles out “the very one”; “이야” just grants the point.

pair.en: I'm fine (at least).
I'm the one who should apologize.

pitfalls.note: The clause that follows is normally a contrast.
pitfalls.en: I write well, but I'm clumsy at speaking.

pitfalls.note: After a vowel the particle is “야”.
pitfalls.en: I'm fine, but I'm worried about the others.

label: as a rule; for a
meaning_en: A particle with two uses. It says that without exception all X are so (“as a rule, there is no X that is not…”), or that something is exceptional for its kind (“for an X, it's surprisingly…”).
usage: It attaches to nouns. In the first sense the clause that follows is almost always negative or a rhetorical question (“없다”, “아닌”), as in “한국 사람치고 김치를 모르는 사람은 없다”. In the second the noun names a category and the clause that follows is a surprising feature, and “치고는” is common (“겨울 날씨치고는 따뜻하다”). It is used in speech and writing.

examples.ko: 한국 사람치고 김치를 모르는 사람은 없다.
examples.en: There is no Korean who doesn't know kimchi.

examples.ko: 아이들치고 놀이터를 싫어하는 아이는 없다.
examples.en: There is no child who dislikes a playground.

examples.ko: 겨울 날씨치고는 제법 따뜻한 편이다.
examples.en: For winter weather, it is rather warm.

examples.ko: 이 식당은 관광지에 있는 가게치고 가격이 착하다.
examples.en: For a shop in a tourist area, this restaurant has fair prices.

examples.ko: 초보치고 운전을 꽤 잘하시네요.
examples.en: You drive quite well for a beginner.

compare.difference: “치고” says there is no exception to the whole group; a plain statement does not rule out an exception.

pair.ko: 한국 사람치고 김치를 모르는 사람은 없다.
pair.en: There is no Korean who doesn't know kimchi.
Most Koreans know kimchi.

compare.difference: “치고” says it is surprising for that kind of thing; “에 비하여” states a comparison to something.

pair.en: It's warm for winter weather.
It's warm compared to last year.

pitfalls.note: In the “no exception” sense the clause that follows is negative.
pitfalls.wrong: 한국 사람치고 김치를 아는 사람이 많다.
pitfalls.right: 한국 사람치고 김치를 모르는 사람은 없다.
pitfalls.en: There is no Korean who doesn't know kimchi.

label: even, on top of that
meaning_en: A particle meaning “even, as well as, on top of that”: it adds one more thing to what is already so, or names a case that goes beyond the usual or expected extent.
usage: It attaches to nouns and to nominalised verbs (“착하기까지 하다”), and to adverbs such as “그렇게까지”. In the additive use it goes with “-ㄴ/은 데다가” or a first item (“바람까지 불었다”), and in the extent use it marks the surprising limit (“거짓말까지 했다”). “까지도” is possible. It is different from the time or place limit “까지” of the level 1 list.

examples.ko: 이 노트북은 가볍고 얇은 데다 성능까지 좋다.
examples.en: This laptop is light and thin, and its performance is good as well.

examples.ko: 지수는 예쁘고 착하기까지 해서 인기가 많다.
examples.en: Jisu is pretty and even kind, so Jisu is very popular.

examples.ko: 비가 오는데 바람까지 불어서 우산이 뒤집어졌다.
examples.en: It was raining and the wind blew on top of that, so my umbrella turned inside out.

examples.ko: 그렇게까지 말할 필요는 없었잖아.
examples.en: There was no need to go as far as saying that.

examples.ko: 친구에게 돈까지 빌려 줬는데 연락이 없다.
examples.en: I even lent money to my friend, and there is no word from them.

compare.difference: “마저” adds the last remaining thing and is mostly used for bad news; “까지” adds without that last-straw feeling.

pair.en: It was raining and the wind blew too.
It was raining and even the wind blew, the last straw.

compare.difference: “도” just adds another; “까지” says the addition goes beyond what was expected.

pair.en: I lent money to the friend too.
I even lent money to the friend.

pitfalls.note: A verb or adjective takes “-기” before “까지”.
pitfalls.en: They are pretty and even kind, so they are very popular.

label: even, at least; second best
meaning_en: A particle for the second-best choice or a minimal option: “even if only X, at least X, X will do”. It also marks “any at all” after a question word, and “even tomorrow, even one” after a time or number.
usage: It attaches to nouns as “이라도” after a final consonant and “라도” after a vowel (“차라도”). In the main sense it offers or accepts an option that is not ideal (“커피라도 한잔하세요”, “지금이라도 시작하자”). It also follows time and quantity words to stress them (“내일이라도”, “한 번이라도”) and question words (“무엇이라도”). The clause that follows is often a request, a suggestion or a wish.

examples.ko: 시간이 없으면 커피라도 한 잔 마시고 가세요.
examples.en: If you have no time, at least have a cup of coffee before you go.

examples.ko: 배고픈데 오면서 라면이라도 사다 줄래?
examples.en: I'm hungry. Could you pick up some ramen, at least, on your way?

examples.ko: 늦었지만 지금이라도 시작해 보자.
examples.en: It is late, but let's start even now.

examples.ko: 어떤 일이라도 해 보겠다는 각오로 면접을 봤다.
examples.en: I went to the interview with the resolve to do any job at all.

examples.ko: 마음만 먹으면 내일이라도 떠날 수 있다.
examples.en: If I make up my mind, I can leave even tomorrow.

compare.difference: “이라도” offers or asks for the next best thing; “이나마” accepts what is modest.

pair.en: Rest, even if only briefly.
I'm glad I could rest, if only briefly.

compare.difference: With a question word the two are close in meaning, but “이라도” can also mean “at least”.

pair.en: Anything at all will do.
Anything is fine.

pitfalls.note: After a vowel the particle is “라도”.
pitfalls.en: Have at least a cup of tea.

label: as, in the capacity of
meaning_en: A particle that names the status, position or qualification in which someone acts or is judged: “as a teacher, as a parent, in the role of X”.
usage: It attaches to nouns of people and roles as “으로서” after a final consonant, and “로서” after a vowel or ㄹ (“교사로서”). It can also name what a place or thing is (“문화 중심지로서”). The clause that follows says what one does, ought to do or is, in that capacity. It is not the “으로써” of means, which is spelled almost the same.

examples.ko: 나는 선생님으로서 아이들의 모범이 되기 위해 노력한다.
examples.en: As a teacher, I try to be a model for the children.

examples.ko: 부모로서 아이의 잘못을 모른 척할 수는 없다.
examples.en: As a parent, I cannot pretend not to see my child's mistake.

examples.ko: 이 도시는 문화 중심지로서 오랜 역사를 가지고 있다.
examples.en: As a cultural center, this city has a long history.

examples.ko: 한 사람의 시민으로서 투표에 꼭 참여해야 한다.
examples.en: As a citizen, one must take part in voting.

examples.ko: 팀장으로서 이번 일의 책임을 지겠습니다.
examples.en: As team leader, I will take responsibility for this matter.

compare.difference: “으로서” says in what capacity; “으로써” says by what means.

pair.en: I teach my child as a parent.
I teach my child by means of love.

compare.difference: In the sense of status the two are close in meaning, and “으로” is the shorter form.

pair.en: I attended the meeting as a representative.
I attended the meeting as a representative.

pitfalls.note: After a vowel the particle is “로서”.
pitfalls.en: I am speaking as a teacher.

pitfalls.note: Do not use the “로써” of means when you mean a capacity.
pitfalls.en: I am speaking as a teacher.

label: by means of, with
meaning_en: A particle for the means, method or material of an action: “by, with, by means of X”. After a verb noun it means “by doing”, and with a time or count it means “as of, with this”.
usage: It attaches to nouns as “으로써” after a final consonant and “로써” after a vowel or ㄹ (“칼로써”). With a verb it takes the nominal form (“운동함으로써”). Before a time or a number it marks a total as of that point (“이번으로써 세 번째”). It is the formal, written choice, and “(으)로” also does the job of means. It is not the “으로서” of status.

examples.ko: 우리는 대화로써 문제를 해결하기로 했다.
examples.en: We decided to resolve the problem by means of dialogue.

examples.ko: 폭력으로써 얻은 평화는 오래가지 못한다.
examples.en: Peace won by violence does not last.

examples.ko: 꾸준히 운동함으로써 건강을 지킬 수 있다.
examples.en: You can keep healthy by exercising steadily.

examples.ko: 이번 계약으로써 우리 회사는 세계 시장에 진출하게 되었다.
examples.en: With this contract, our company has come to enter the world market.

examples.ko: 시험에 떨어진 것도 이번으로써 세 번째다.
examples.en: This makes the third time I have failed an exam.

compare.difference: “으로써” says by what means; “으로서” says in what capacity.

pair.en: I teach my child by means of love.
I teach my child as a parent.

compare.difference: For means the two are close in meaning; “으로” is the everyday form, “으로써” the written one.

pair.en: I cut the paper with a knife.
I cut the paper with a knife.

pitfalls.note: A means is not marked by the “로서” of status.
pitfalls.en: We resolved the problem by means of dialogue.

pitfalls.note: After a noun ending in ㄹ, the form is “로써”.
pitfalls.en: I cut the paper with a knife.

label: even, the last one too
meaning_en: A particle meaning “even, too, the last one as well”: it adds the one thing still remaining to what has already happened, most often another loss or another blow.
usage: It attaches to nouns, and it replaces the subject and object particles, so it is not followed by “이/가” or “을/를”. It is used for the last remaining item (“가장 친한 친구마저”, “바람마저”), usually in a negative or unfortunate situation, although a neutral use also exists (“남은 숙제마저 끝냈다”). It is different from the adverb “마저” (“finish the rest”).

examples.ko: 추운데 바람마저 불어서 밖에 다니기가 힘들다.
examples.en: It is cold and the wind blows on top of that, so it is hard to be out.

examples.ko: 가장 친한 친구마저 나를 믿어 주지 않았다.
examples.en: Even my closest friend did not believe me.

examples.ko: 비가 많이 와서 도로마저 침수되었다.
examples.en: It rained so much that even the roads were flooded.

examples.ko: 시력마저 나빠져서 책을 읽기가 힘들어졌다.
examples.en: Even my eyesight got worse, so it became hard to read.

examples.ko: 건강마저 잃고 나서야 나는 쉬는 법을 배웠다.
examples.en: Only after losing even my health did I learn how to rest.

compare.difference: “조차” picks the most unexpected case; “마저” adds the last one that was left.

pair.en: Even my family, the last I had, did not believe me.
Even my family, of all people, did not believe me.

compare.difference: “까지” adds a thing without implying a last straw; “마저” suggests the last one was lost or added.

pair.en: It was raining and the wind blew too.
It was raining and even the wind blew.

pitfalls.note: It replaces the subject particle; it does not stack on it.
pitfalls.en: Even my friend left.

label: not only, and also
meaning_en: A literary connective ending that acknowledges the first fact and adds a related one: “X is so, and moreover Y; not only X but also Y”. It sometimes introduces a fact that everyone knows.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems as “-거니와” (“좋거니와”, “있거니와”), to “이다” as “이거니와”, and after “-었-” and “-겠-” (“앞서 말했거니와”, “다시 말하겠거니와”), but not after the modifier “-을/-ㄹ”. Both clauses point the same way, and the first often carries “도” (“맛도 좋거니와 값도 싸다”). The dictionary labels it as old-fashioned speech, and it is used in formal writing rather than in conversation.

examples.ko: 이 책은 내용도 훌륭하거니와 디자인도 아름답다.
examples.en: This book has excellent contents and a beautiful design too.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 성격도 좋거니와 실력도 뛰어나다.
examples.en: That person has a good character and is also highly skilled.

examples.ko: 날씨도 춥거니와 길도 미끄러워서 조심해야 한다.
examples.en: It is cold and the road is slippery too, so you have to be careful.

examples.ko: 시간도 없거니와 돈도 부족해서 여행은 포기했다.
examples.en: I had no time and not enough money either, so I gave up on the trip.

examples.ko: 누구나 아는 사실이거니와 이 문제는 하루아침에 해결되지 않는다.
examples.en: As everyone knows, this problem will not be solved overnight.

compare.difference: Both mean “not only … but also”; “-거니와” is the more literary of the two.

pair.en: It tastes good, and the price is low too.
It not only tastes good but is cheap too.

compare.difference: “-고” just lists; “-거니와” admits the first point and adds another.

pair.en: It tastes good and is cheap.
It tastes good, and the price is low too.

pitfalls.note: It takes no future “-ㄹ” before it.
pitfalls.en: This place is tasty and cheap too.

label: even though; and also
meaning_en: A connective ending that joins a fact with another that is contrary to it, or adds a further quality: “even after doing X, still Y; being X and also Y”.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems as “-고도” (“알고도”, “작고도”). With verbs of knowing, seeing and hearing it means “even though one has done it”, and the clause that follows is the unexpected one (“알고도 모른 척하다”). With adjectives it joins two qualities (“작고도 아늑하다”). Both clauses share a subject, and it is written as one word.

examples.ko: 그 사실을 알고도 아무 말도 하지 않았다.
examples.en: Even though I knew that fact, I did not say a word.

examples.ko: 이 방은 작고도 아늑하다.
examples.en: This room is small and also cozy.

examples.ko: 밥을 먹고도 배가 고프다.
examples.en: Even after eating, I am hungry.

examples.ko: 지수는 모든 것을 잃고도 웃을 수 있는 사람이다.
examples.en: Jisu is someone who can smile even after losing everything.

examples.ko: 힘들고도 보람 있는 일이다.
examples.en: It is hard and rewarding work.

compare.difference: “-는데도” can have different subjects in the two clauses; “-고도” needs the same subject.

pair.en: I laughed even after getting wet in the rain.
Even though I got wet in the rain, I laughed.

compare.difference: “-지만” is a plain “but”; “-고도” stresses that one did X and yet Y.

pair.en: I knew, but I didn't say.
Knowing, I still did not say.

pitfalls.note: Both clauses share one subject.
pitfalls.wrong: 내가 알고도 동생은 아무 말도 하지 않았다.
pitfalls.right: 나는 알고도 아무 말도 하지 않았다.
pitfalls.en: Even though I knew, I did not say a word.

label: in order to, aiming to
meaning_en: A formal connective ending for purpose or intention: “in order to, intending to, hoping to”. It tells the aim of the action in the main clause.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-고자” (no “으”), and it takes no tense. The same subject does both actions. It is used in speeches, announcements, applications and reports, and “-고자 하다” is the formal way to state one's intention (“말씀드리고자 합니다”). It is not used for ordinary conversation.

examples.ko: 저는 이 자리를 빌려 감사의 말씀을 드리고자 합니다.
examples.en: I would like to take this opportunity to express my thanks.

examples.ko: 문제를 해결하고자 전문가를 초청했다.
examples.en: We invited experts in order to resolve the problem.

examples.ko: 건강을 지키고자 매일 아침 운동을 하고 있다.
examples.en: I exercise every morning in order to keep healthy.

examples.ko: 이번 연구는 한국어 교육의 효과를 확인하고자 진행되었다.
examples.en: This study was carried out in order to confirm the effect of Korean-language education.

examples.ko: 자세한 내용을 알리고자 안내문을 보냅니다.
examples.en: We are sending a notice in order to give you the details.

compare.difference: The two are close in meaning; “-고자” is the form for speeches and writing, “-으려고” the everyday one.

pair.en: I came to Korea to learn Korean.
I came to Korea to learn Korean.

compare.difference: The two are close in meaning; “-기 위해” works with a noun phrase and in more ways.

pair.en: I studied hard to pass.
I studied hard to pass.

pitfalls.note: It takes no tense.
pitfalls.en: I studied hard in order to pass.

label: since, as a basis
meaning_en: A connective ending that gives the reason or basis for the main clause: “since, because, seeing that X”. The clause that follows is the action or conclusion that the reason prompted.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems as “-기에”, to “이다” as “-이기에”, and after “-었-”. The main clause is usually past or a statement of result, and it cannot be a command or a suggestion. The spoken contraction is “-길래”. It is used in speech and writing.

examples.ko: 아침부터 날씨가 흐리기에 우산을 챙겨 나왔다.
examples.en: The weather was cloudy from the morning, so I took an umbrella.

examples.ko: 표정이 어둡기에 무슨 일이 있는지 물어보았다.
examples.en: Their face looked dark, so I asked whether something was wrong.

examples.ko: 그만큼 노력했기에 좋은 결과를 얻을 수 있었다.
examples.en: It was because of that much effort that a good result was possible.

examples.ko: 주민들이 모두 반대했기에 그 계획은 취소되었다.
examples.en: Since the residents all opposed it, the plan was cancelled.

examples.ko: 지금까지 버텨 왔기에 앞으로도 해낼 수 있을 것이다.
examples.en: Since we have held out until now, we will be able to manage from now on too.

compare.difference: “-길래” is the spoken contraction of “-기에”; the two mean the same.

pair.en: Seeing the dark look, I asked.
Seeing the dark look, I asked.

compare.difference: “-으니까” can be followed by a command; “-기에” cannot.

pair.en: It was raining, so I did not go.
It is raining, so don't go.

pitfalls.note: The clause that follows cannot be a command.
pitfalls.en: It was cold, so I wore a coat out.

label: whether, how, why (indirect question)
meaning_en: A connective ending that turns a question into part of a larger sentence: “whether, how, why, what X is”. It can also give a vague reason or judgement: “perhaps because X, …”. As a final ending it asks an uncertain question.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-는지”, to adjective stems as “-ㄴ/은지”, to “이다” as “인지”, and the past is “-었는지”; future or conjecture is “-ㄹ지”. It is followed by verbs of knowing, asking and wondering (“알다”, “모르다”, “궁금하다”, “묻다”). In the vague-reason use (“얼마나 열심히 일했는지 얼굴이 야위었다”) the clause that follows shows a result.

examples.ko: 그 사람이 어디에 사는지 아세요?
examples.en: Do you know where that person lives?

examples.ko: 왜 그런지 모르겠지만 요즘 자꾸 졸려요.
examples.en: I don't know why, but I keep feeling sleepy lately.

examples.ko: 오늘 시험이 어려운지 쉬운지 아직 모르겠다.
examples.en: I still don't know whether today's exam is hard or easy.

examples.ko: 얼마나 열심히 일했는지 얼굴이 많이 야위었다.
examples.en: They have worked so hard that their face has grown quite thin.

examples.ko: 내일 비가 올지 안 올지 확인해 봐.
examples.en: Check whether it will rain tomorrow or not.

compare.difference: “-을까” is a question asked in a sentence of its own; “-는지” builds the question into a sentence.

pair.en: Will it rain tomorrow?
I don't know whether it will rain tomorrow.

compare.difference: “-는지” is an indirect question; “-냐고” quotes the asking.

pair.en: I asked where they were going.
I asked, “Where are you going?”

pitfalls.note: An adjective takes “-ㄴ/은지”.
pitfalls.en: I don't know whether the weather is good.

label: as you know; almost
meaning_en: A connective ending with two uses: “as you (already) know, see, can tell”, and “almost, practically doing X”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-다시피”, with no tense. In the first use it goes with verbs of knowing and perception (“아시다시피”, “보시다시피”, “알다시피”) and the clause that follows rests on what the listener already knows. In the second it goes with “-다시피 하다” (“살다시피 하다”) to say that something is nearly the same as the act. A ㄹ-stem keeps its ㄹ (“살다시피”).

examples.ko: 여러분도 아시다시피 올해는 경기가 좋지 않습니다.
examples.en: As you all know, the economy is not good this year.

examples.ko: 보시다시피 제 방은 아주 좁아요.
examples.en: As you can see, my room is very small.

examples.ko: 알다시피 나는 매운 음식을 못 먹어.
examples.en: As you know, I can't eat spicy food.

examples.ko: 시험 기간에는 도서관에서 살다시피 했다.
examples.en: During exam period I practically lived in the library.

examples.ko: 민준이는 요즘 매일 야근을 하다시피 한다.
examples.en: Minjun works late practically every day these days.

compare.difference: “-는 바와 같이” is the formal “as”; “-다시피” is shorter and goes with “알다”, “보다” and the like.

pair.en: As you can see, the situation is hard.
As you can see, the situation is hard.

compare.difference: “-다시피 하다” says something comes close to the act; “-ㄴ 셈이다” says it amounts to it.

pair.en: I practically lived there.
It amounts to having lived there.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem keeps its ㄹ, and the form without it is a different verb.
pitfalls.en: I practically lived in the library.

label: even if, granting
meaning_en: A connective ending for a concession: “even if X, still Y”. It assumes or grants a situation and says the main clause holds regardless.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems as “-더라도”, to “이다” as “이더라도”, and after “-었-”. It supposes a situation, and the main clause may be a command, a suggestion, a decision or a statement, since it is not bound by the first clause. “아무리” and “설령” often come before it. It is used in speech and writing.

examples.ko: 힘들더라도 끝까지 포기하지 마세요.
examples.en: Even if it is hard, please don't give up; see it through.

examples.ko: 비가 오더라도 행사는 예정대로 진행합니다.
examples.en: Even if it rains, the event will go ahead as scheduled.

examples.ko: 아무리 바쁘더라도 아침은 꼭 챙겨 먹어요.
examples.en: No matter how busy you are, be sure to eat breakfast.

examples.ko: 실패하더라도 도전해 볼 가치는 있다.
examples.en: Even if you fail, it is worth taking up the challenge.

examples.ko: 설령 틀렸더라도 부끄러워할 필요는 없다.
examples.en: Even if you were wrong, there is no need to feel ashamed.

compare.difference: The two are close in meaning; “-더라도” more clearly supposes a situation, while “-아도/어도” can also state a fact.

pair.en: I go even if it rains.
I will go even if it rains.

compare.difference: Both are concessive; “-을지라도” is the form for formal writing.

pair.en: Even if it's hard, try it.
Though it is hard, try it.

pitfalls.note: It supposes a situation; it does not report an actual past event.
pitfalls.en: Even if it rains tomorrow, I will go.

label: either one, whichever
meaning_en: A connective ending for choosing between alternatives or for saying that any of them will do: “whether X or Y, either X or Y, whichever”. With a question word it means “whatever, whoever”.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems and to “이다” (“이든지”), usually repeated in pairs (“가든지 말든지”, “오든지 가든지”). The shortened “-든” is the same. Joined to a question word it gives “무엇을 하든지”, “누가 오든지”. The clause that follows is the decision, a command or a statement that does not depend on the choice. It is not the “-던” of recalled experience.

examples.ko: 가든지 말든지 네 마음대로 해.
examples.en: Go or don't go, do as you like.

examples.ko: 비가 오든지 눈이 오든지 약속은 지켜야 한다.
examples.en: Rain or snow, a promise has to be kept.

examples.ko: 책을 읽든지 영화를 보든지 편한 대로 하세요.
examples.en: Read a book or watch a movie, whichever you like.

examples.ko: 무엇을 하든지 최선을 다해라.
examples.en: Whatever you do, do your best.

examples.ko: 누가 오든지 상관없으니 문은 열어 두세요.
examples.en: It doesn't matter who comes, so leave the door open.

compare.difference: “-거나” lists alternatives that really occur or are chosen; “-든지” says it is up to you, any will do.

pair.en: On weekends I read a book or watch a movie.
Read a book or watch a movie, as you like.

compare.difference: The two are close in meaning and are used in the same way.

pair.en: Go or don't, do as you like.
Go or don't, do as you like.

pitfalls.note: Do not confuse “-든지” (choice) with “-던지” (recalled experience).
pitfalls.en: Read a book or watch a movie, as you like.

label: since, therefore (formal)
meaning_en: A formal connective ending giving a reason or cause: “since, because, therefore”. It is the written counterpart of “-으니까” and “-아서” and is common in announcements, rules, reports and arguments.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems as “-으므로”, or “-므로” after a vowel or ㄹ (“살므로”, “바쁘므로”), to “이다” as “이므로”, and after “-었-” (“내렸으므로”). The main clause states the conclusion or measure that follows. It is formal and written, so in conversation “-으니까” or “-아서” is used. The neutral “-기 때문에” is a close equivalent.

examples.ko: 내일은 휴일이므로 도서관이 문을 닫습니다.
examples.en: Tomorrow is a holiday, so the library will be closed.

examples.ko: 비가 많이 내렸으므로 오늘 경기는 취소되었습니다.
examples.en: It rained heavily, so today's game has been cancelled.

examples.ko: 사람은 사회적 동물이므로 혼자서는 살 수 없다.
examples.en: Humans are social animals, so they cannot live alone.

examples.ko: 이 방법이 가장 효율적이므로 우리는 이를 채택하기로 했다.
examples.en: This method is the most efficient, so we decided to adopt it.

examples.ko: 피해가 심각하므로 정부는 긴급 지원을 결정했다.
examples.en: The damage was serious, so the government decided on emergency aid.

compare.difference: The two are close in meaning; “-으므로” is the form for written and formal language.

pair.en: The damage is serious, so aid is needed.
The damage is serious, so aid is needed.

compare.difference: “-으니까” can lead into a command or a suggestion; “-으므로” leads into a conclusion.

pair.en: It is a holiday, so we are closed.
It is a holiday, so take a rest.

pitfalls.note: After “이다” the ending is “이므로”.
pitfalls.en: Tomorrow is a holiday, so we are closed.

pitfalls.note: A stem ending in ㄹ takes “-므로”, with no “으”.
pitfalls.wrong: 사람은 사회 속에서 살으므로 서로 도와야 한다.
pitfalls.right: 사람은 사회 속에서 살므로 서로 도와야 한다.
pitfalls.en: People live within society, so they must help one another.

label: even if I want to, I can't
meaning_en: A colloquial connective ending that says one has the wish to do something, yet cannot: “even if I wanted to X, I can't”. The verb is repeated in the main clause.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-을래야”, or “-ㄹ래야” after a vowel or ㄹ (“갈래야”, “잊을래야”), and the same verb is repeated with “-ㄹ 수 없다”, “-ㄹ 수가 없다”, “못 -” or “-ㄹ 방법이 없다”. The main clause is always a denial of ability or possibility. It is the everyday spoken form of “-으려야”; the standard dictionaries accept only “-으려야” (“잊으려야 잊을 수 없다”), so that is the spelling for formal writing.

examples.ko: 그 장면은 잊을래야 잊을 수가 없다.
examples.en: I can't forget that scene even if I try.

examples.ko: 너무 바빠서 쉴래야 쉴 시간이 없다.
examples.en: I'm so busy that I have no time to rest even if I wanted to.

examples.ko: 돈이 없어서 살래야 살 수 없었다.
examples.en: I had no money, so I couldn't have bought it even if I wanted to.

examples.ko: 연락처를 몰라서 연락할래야 할 방법이 없었다.
examples.en: I didn't know their contact details, so I had no way to get in touch even if I wanted to.

examples.ko: 길이 막혀서 갈래야 갈 수가 없어요.
examples.en: The roads are jammed, so I can't go even if I want to.

compare.difference: The same expression: “-으려야” is the standard spelling, and “-을래야” is how most people say it.

pair.en: I can't forget even if I try.
I can't forget even if I try.

compare.difference: “-고 싶어도” says one wants to but is blocked; “-을래야” repeats the verb to stress that there is no way.

pair.en: Even if I want to go, I can't.
I can't go even if I try.

pitfalls.note: The main clause has to deny possibility.
pitfalls.en: I can't go even if I want to.

label: after doing; unless; yet
meaning_en: A connective ending with three uses: an action done and finished before the next one (“after doing X”), a condition in “-고서는 … 없다” (“not without X”), and a contrast between what one did and what followed (“having done X, yet Y”). “-고서야” means “only after”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-고서”, and it can add “는” or “야”. In the sequence use, the first action is complete and often the cause or precondition of the next. “-고서는” is followed by a negative or impossible statement (“노력하지 않고서는 해낼 수 없다”). “-고서야” says that only after X could Y happen (“해 보고서야 알았다”). It is used in speech and writing.

examples.ko: 지수는 문을 열고서 한참 동안 밖을 바라보았다.
examples.en: Jisu opened the door and looked outside for a long while.

examples.ko: 밥을 먹고서 약을 드세요.
examples.en: Take the medicine after you eat.

examples.ko: 이 일은 노력하지 않고서는 해낼 수 없다.
examples.en: This job cannot be done without effort.

examples.ko: 직접 해 보고서야 그 어려움을 알게 되었다.
examples.en: Only after trying it myself did I come to know how hard it was.

examples.ko: 사실을 알고서 모르는 척하는 것은 옳지 않다.
examples.en: It is not right to pretend not to know after you have learned the truth.

compare.difference: “-고” simply links; “-고서” stresses that the first action is finished before the second.

pair.en: I washed my hands and ate.
I washed my hands first, and then ate.

compare.difference: The two are close in meaning; “-고 나서” makes the completion explicit.

pair.en: I took the medicine after eating.
I took the medicine after I finished eating.

pitfalls.note: “-고서는” goes with a negative or impossible main clause.
pitfalls.en: Without effort you cannot succeed.

label: if (supposing that)
meaning_en: A connective ending for a supposition: “if, supposing that, in case X”. It sets up a supposed situation, often an imagined or unlikely one.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-ㄴ다면/-는다면”, to adjective stems and past forms as “-다면” (“좋다면”, “갔다면”), and to “이다” as “-라면” (“학생이라면”). It suits supposed, hypothetical or reported situations, and the main clause can state a wish, a plan or a judgement. The “-었다면” form speaks of a past that did not happen or an assumed past. It is used in speech and writing.

examples.ko: 내가 새가 된다면 너에게 가장 먼저 날아갈 거야.
examples.en: If I became a bird, I would fly to you first.

examples.ko: 만약 내일 비가 온다면 소풍은 취소하겠습니다.
examples.en: If it should rain tomorrow, I will cancel the picnic.

examples.ko: 복권에 당첨된다면 무엇을 하고 싶어요?
examples.en: If you won the lottery, what would you want to do?

examples.ko: 네가 그렇게 원한다면 한번 해 보자.
examples.en: If you want it that badly, let's give it a try.

examples.ko: 그 말이 사실이라면 큰 문제가 된다.
examples.en: If that is true, it becomes a big problem.

compare.difference: “-으면” is the plain, general condition; “-는다면” supposes a situation, often an imagined one.

pair.en: If it rains, we cancel.
If it should rain, I will cancel.

pitfalls.note: After “이다” the form is “-라면”, not “-ㄴ다면”.
pitfalls.en: If that person is a student, I'll be surprised.

pitfalls.note: An adjective takes “-다면”, with no “-ㄴ”.
pitfalls.en: If the weather is good, we will go on a picnic.

label: I observed, and then
meaning_en: A connective ending that links something the speaker observed in the past with what followed or with a new situation: “X did/was, and then Y”. It can state a result of the observed action, a change from before, or a contrast with before.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems as “-더니”, and to “이다” as “이더니”. The observer is the speaker, and the subject of the first clause is normally someone else, or the speaker's own state that is felt as observed. The second clause tells what followed, usually in the past. It cannot be followed by a command or a suggestion. It is used in speech and writing.

examples.ko: 아침에는 맑더니 오후부터 흐려지기 시작했다.
examples.en: It was clear in the morning, but it began to cloud over from the afternoon.

examples.ko: 지수는 열심히 공부하더니 결국 합격했다.
examples.en: Jisu studied hard and in the end passed.

examples.ko: 어제는 그렇게 춥더니 오늘은 따뜻하네요.
examples.en: It was so cold yesterday, but it is warm today.

examples.ko: 아이가 너무 많이 먹더니 배탈이 났다.
examples.en: The child ate too much and got a stomachache.

examples.ko: 민준이는 방에 들어가더니 한참 동안 나오지 않았다.
examples.en: Minjun went into the room and did not come out for a long while.

compare.difference: “-았더니” reports the speaker's own act and the result; “-더니” reports what someone else did and what followed.

pair.en: Jisu took the medicine and got better.
I took the medicine and got better.

compare.difference: “-다가” says an action was interrupted or switched; “-더니” links an observed action with its result or change.

pair.en: I fell asleep while reading.

pair.ko: 동생은 책을 읽더니 갑자기 웃기 시작했다.
pair.en: My younger sibling read the book and then suddenly started laughing.

pitfalls.note: The subject is not the speaker; for one's own act use “-았더니/었더니”.
pitfalls.en: Jisu studied hard and passed.

label: I saw that, and so
meaning_en: A connective ending that gives something the speaker saw or experienced in the past as background for what comes next: a suggestion, a question, or a contrast. As a final ending, “-던데(요)” voices the speaker's impression and invites a response.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems as “-던데”, to “이다” as “이던데”, and after “-었-” (“왔던데”). The speaker has experienced the fact directly, so a fact that was only heard is not given this way. The clause that follows is a suggestion, a question, a conclusion or a contrast (“어제는 잘 먹던데 오늘은 왜 안 먹어?”). It is spoken and written in a casual way.

examples.ko: 그 영화 재미있던데 같이 볼래요?
examples.en: That movie was good; do you want to watch it together?

examples.ko: 어제 보니 지수가 일찍 가던데 오늘은 회사에 있네요.
examples.en: I saw Jisu leave early yesterday, but today they are at the office.

examples.ko: 날씨가 좋던데 산책이나 할까요?
examples.en: The weather was nice, so shall we go for a walk?

examples.ko: 그 가게에는 사람이 많던데 줄을 서야 할 거예요.
examples.en: There were a lot of people at that shop, so you'll probably have to wait in line.

examples.ko: 어제는 잘 먹던데 오늘은 왜 안 먹어?
examples.en: You ate well yesterday; why aren't you eating today?

compare.difference: “-는데” gives present background; “-던데” gives something the speaker experienced earlier.

pair.en: That movie is good; do you want to watch it together?
That movie was good (I saw it); do you want to watch it together?

compare.difference: “-더라고” just reports what was found; “-던데” gives it as background to what comes next.

pair.en: That movie was good.
That movie was good; do you want to watch it together?

pitfalls.note: It is “-던데”, not “-든데”.
pitfalls.en: That movie was good; do you want to watch it together?

label: just as, as if
meaning_en: A connective ending meaning “just as, like, as if”: the main clause is nearly the same as what the first clause describes, either as a comparison or as a manner (“as if X”).
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems as “-듯이”, to “이다” as “이듯이”, and the adnominal forms “-ㄴ/는 듯이” and “-었듯이” also occur. The first clause gives a familiar picture (“물 흐르듯이”, “비 오듯이”), or says that something is done as if X (“아무 일도 없었다는 듯이”). “-듯” is the shortened form. It is common in essays and narration.

examples.ko: 물이 흐르듯이 자연스럽게 말해야 한다.
examples.en: You should speak as naturally as water flows.

examples.ko: 더운 날씨에 땀이 비 오듯이 흘렀다.
examples.en: In the hot weather, sweat poured down like rain.

examples.ko: 밥 먹듯이 거짓말을 하는 사람은 믿을 수 없다.
examples.en: A person who lies as easily as eating a meal cannot be trusted.

examples.ko: 봄이 오면 꽃이 피듯이 노력하면 결실을 얻는다.
examples.en: Just as flowers bloom when spring comes, effort bears fruit.

examples.ko: 아무 일도 없었다는 듯이 지수는 웃으며 들어왔다.
examples.en: As if nothing had happened, Jisu came in smiling.

compare.difference: The two are close in meaning; “-듯이” is the one you see in set images and in prose.

pair.en: They talk as if they know.
They talk as if they know.

compare.difference: “-듯” is the shortened form of “-듯이”, with the same meaning.

pair.en: I spoke as smoothly as water flows.
I spoke as smoothly as water flows.

pitfalls.note: It needs a verb, not a bare noun: “밥 먹듯이”, not “밥듯이”.
pitfalls.en: They lie as easily as eating a meal.

label: the more, the more
meaning_en: A connective ending meaning “the more X, the more Y”: as the degree of the first clause increases, the second changes along with it.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems as “-을수록”, or “-ㄹ수록” after a vowel or ㄹ (“알수록”, “바쁠수록”, “들수록”), and to “이다” as “일수록”. It has no tense before it. The main clause tells what changes, often with “더”, “더욱” or “-아/어지다”. The first clause is usually repeated in the main clause as the same word or its contrast (“알면 알수록”). It is common in essays and sayings.

examples.ko: 알면 알수록 더 알고 싶어진다.
examples.en: The more I know, the more I want to know.

examples.ko: 날씨가 추울수록 따뜻한 국물이 생각난다.
examples.en: The colder the weather, the more I think of a warm broth.

examples.ko: 나이가 들수록 시간이 빨리 가는 것 같다.
examples.en: The older I get, the faster time seems to go.

examples.ko: 사람은 가까울수록 예의를 지켜야 한다.
examples.en: The closer people are, the more they should keep up good manners.

examples.ko: 급할수록 천천히 돌아가라는 말이 있다.
examples.en: There is a saying that the more pressed you are, the more you should take the long way round.

compare.difference: “-을 만큼” makes the second clause equal to the first; “-을수록” makes it grow along with the first.

pair.en: I gain weight in proportion to what I eat.
The more I eat, the more weight I gain.

compare.difference: “-을 때마다” says it happens each time; “-을수록” says it grows as the degree rises.

pair.en: Mistakes occur every time I'm busy.
The busier I am, the more mistakes increase.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem takes “-ㄹ수록”, not “-을수록”.
pitfalls.en: The more I know, the more I want to know.

label: while doing; and
meaning_en: A written connective ending with two uses: two actions or states at the same time (“while doing X, Y”), and a plain listing of facts or qualities (“X, and also Y”).
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems as “-으며”, or “-며” after a vowel or ㄹ (“웃으며”, “노래하며”, “살며”), and to “이다” as “이며”. In the simultaneous use the two actions belong to one subject. In the listing use it joins two or more facts of the same kind. It does not mark a sequence. It is formal or written, and “-으면서” is the spoken equivalent.

examples.ko: 지수는 노래를 부르며 길을 걸었다.
examples.en: Jisu walked along the road singing.

examples.ko: 이 도시는 역사가 깊으며 문화유산이 풍부하다.
examples.en: This city has a long history and rich cultural heritage.

examples.ko: 아이들은 웃으며 뛰어놀았다.
examples.en: The children played, laughing.

examples.ko: 나는 커피를 마시며 신문을 읽었다.
examples.en: I read the newspaper while drinking coffee.

examples.ko: 이분은 의사이며 작가이다.
examples.en: This person is a doctor and a writer.

compare.difference: The two are close in meaning; “-으며” is the form for written language.

pair.en: I walked listening to music.
I walked listening to music.

compare.difference: “-고” can mark a sequence (one action, then the next); “-으며” marks things happening together or things listed.

pair.en: I listened to music and then ate.
I ate while listening to music.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem takes “-며”, with no “으”.
pitfalls.en: They grew old living happily.

label: how on earth…? puzzled question
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending that takes a fact as given and questions it, usually with a question word and a note of puzzlement or complaint: “how on earth…?, why is it that…?, when are we ever going to…?”. It is less a request for information than the speaker wondering aloud.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-ㄴ다니/-는다니” (“읽는다니”, “간다니”), to adjective stems and past forms as “-다니” (“춥다니”, “잤다니”), and to “이다” as “-라니”. It usually goes with a question word (“어떻게”, “언제”, “왜”, “누가”) and rising intonation. It is plain speech (krdict: “아주낮춤”), heard mostly from an older speaker to a younger listener or when talking to oneself, and it has no polite form. Do not confuse it with the surprised echo “-다니요?” (level-4 “-다니1”), which repeats what was just said.

examples.ko: 밥을 먹고 어떻게 바로 눕는다니?
examples.en: How can you lie down right after eating?

examples.ko: 대체 우리는 언제 저녁을 먹는다니?
examples.en: When on earth are we going to eat dinner?

examples.ko: 이렇게 비가 오는데 어떻게 소풍을 간다니?
examples.en: It's raining like this; how can we go on a picnic?

examples.ko: 너희 반은 왜 그렇게 시끄럽다니?
examples.en: Why on earth is your class so noisy?

examples.ko: 추석이 지난 지가 언제인데 아직도 이렇게 덥다니?
examples.en: Chuseok is long past; how can it still be this hot?

compare.difference: “-을까?” wonders neutrally; “-는다니?” takes the fact as given and questions it, often with a hint of complaint.

pair.en: How should this be read, I wonder?
How on earth do you read this?

compare.difference: The echo “-다니요?” repeats what was just said, in surprise, and can be polite; “-는다니?” questions a fact taken as given, usually with a question word, and has no polite form.

pair.en: The traffic is bad? It was fine a while ago.
Why on earth is the traffic so bad?

pitfalls.note: It is plain speech with no polite form; to someone you address politely ask with “-어요?” or “-나요?”.
pitfalls.en: Professor, how do you read this?

pitfalls.note: An adjective takes “-다니”, with no “-는”.
pitfalls.en: Why on earth is it already this cold?

label: I see, I found that
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending for telling a fact the speaker has found out firsthand and noticed with some interest or admiration: “I see, I found that…, it turned out that…”. The polite form is “-더군요”.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems, to “이다” (“이더군”), and after “-었-” and “-겠-”. The speaker must have seen or experienced the fact in person, and it is told as a newly learned thing. The polite form is “-더군요”. It is used in conversation.

examples.ko: 오랜만에 승규를 만났는데 못 본 사이에 키가 많이 컸더군.
examples.en: I met Seunggyu for the first time in a long while, and they had grown a lot in the time I hadn't seen them.

examples.ko: 어제 가 보니 그 식당 음식이 꽤 맛있더군요.
examples.en: I went there yesterday, and the food at that restaurant was quite good.

examples.ko: 내일 열리는 농구 결승전이 꽤 재미있겠더군.
examples.en: Tomorrow's basketball final looks like it will be quite exciting.

examples.ko: 밖에 나가 보니 벌써 눈이 쌓였더군.
examples.en: I went outside, and the snow had already piled up.

examples.ko: 이번 시험은 생각보다 쉽더군.
examples.en: This exam was easier than I thought.

compare.difference: “-네” voices what the speaker has just noticed; “-더군” tells what the speaker found earlier.

pair.en: The food here is good.
The food there was good.

compare.difference: The two are close in meaning; both report a discovery made firsthand.

pair.en: The food there was good.
The food there was good.

pitfalls.note: It reports something the speaker found out, not an act the speaker chose.
pitfalls.right: 어제 도서관에 가 보니 사람들이 공부하고 있더군.
pitfalls.en: I went to the library yesterday, and people were studying.

label: I found it was; what was it?
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending with two uses. It reports something the speaker found out firsthand (“it turned out to be…”), and, as a question, it calls up something half-remembered, asking oneself or someone who shared the experience (“what was it again?”).
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems, to “이다” (“이더라”), and after “-었-”. In the report use the speaker saw or felt the fact and the subject is not the speaker's own decision. In the recall use it is a question to oneself or to someone who was there, usually with a question word (“어디에 뒀더라?”, “우리가 어디서 만났더라?”). It is the plain “해라” level, and the polite form of the report is “-더라고요”.

examples.ko: 오랜만에 가 보니 그 식당 손님이 많이 줄었더라.
examples.en: I went after a long time, and that restaurant's customers had dropped a lot.

examples.ko: 어제 본 영화는 생각보다 슬프더라.
examples.en: The movie I saw yesterday was sadder than I thought.

examples.ko: 그 아이가 벌써 중학생이더라.
examples.en: It turned out that child is already in middle school.

examples.ko: 내 안경을 어디에 뒀더라?
examples.en: Where did I put my glasses again?

examples.ko: 지난번에 우리가 어디서 만났더라?
examples.en: Where was it that we met last time?

compare.difference: The two are close in meaning; “-더라고” can take “요” for polite speech, but “-더라” stays plain.

pair.en: That movie was good.
That movie was good.

compare.difference: In the recall use the two are close in meaning; “-던가” also asks oneself about a half-remembered thing.

pair.en: Where did I put that again?
Where did I put that, now?

pitfalls.note: In the report use it is not for the speaker's own deliberate act.
pitfalls.right: 어제 학교에 가 보니 사람이 없더라.
pitfalls.en: I went to school yesterday, and nobody was there.

label: command, exclamation
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending with two uses: a command to someone of lower standing or to a close friend (“do it”), and, in a monologue, an exclamation of feeling (“how sad!”).
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-아라/-어라”, and the vowel of the stem decides which (“먹어라”, “찾아라”). It contracts with vowel-final stems (“가라”, “와라”, “일어나라”), and “하다” gives “해라”. Irregular stems change as usual (“돕다 → 도와라”). In the exclamation use it attaches to a few feeling adjectives (“슬퍼라”, “부끄러워라”). It is the plain “해라” level, which does not suit speaking to an elder.

examples.ko: 물을 마구 쓰지 말고 아껴 써라.
examples.en: Don't waste water; use it sparingly.

examples.ko: 음식은 충분하니 모두 실컷 먹어라.
examples.en: There is plenty of food, so everyone eat your fill.

examples.ko: 늦겠다. 어서 일어나라.
examples.en: You'll be late. Get up quickly.

examples.ko: 집에 가면 손부터 씻어라.
examples.en: When you get home, wash your hands first.

examples.ko: 아이고, 부끄러워라. 그 사람이 다 봤네.
examples.en: Oh, how embarrassing. That person saw it all.

compare.difference: “-으세요” is the polite command; “-어라” is the plain one for someone younger or close.

pair.en: Get up early.
Please get up early.

compare.difference: Both are commands at the “해라” level; “-거라” sounds like an elder speaking and is most common with a few verbs such as “가다” and “자다”.

pair.en: Go quickly.
Go quickly.

pitfalls.note: “오다” contracts to “와라”, not “오아라”.
pitfalls.en: Come here.

pitfalls.note: A ㅂ-irregular stem becomes “도와라”.
pitfalls.en: Help your mother a bit.

label: guess! rhetorical -ge?
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending that asks a question to which the speaker has a point to make: a guessing quiz (“guess what…!”), a rhetorical question that denies something (“would I really…?”), or a question about the listener's intention. The polite form is “-게요?”.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems, to “이다” (“-이게”), and after “-었-”. In the quiz use it follows a question word (“이게 뭐게?”, “누구를 만났게?”). In the rhetorical use the “-면” clause supposes something absurd and “-게?” rejects it (“공부 안 하고 합격하면 누가 공부하게?”). In the intention use the speaker is surprised at a plan (“그만 드시게요?”). It is spoken with rising intonation and is informal.

examples.ko: 연습도 안 하고 합격하면 누가 공부하게?
examples.en: If you could pass without studying, who would study?

examples.ko: 내가 이번 시험에서 몇 점 받았게?
examples.en: Guess what score I got on this exam.

examples.ko: 오늘 백화점에서 내가 누구를 만났게?
examples.en: Guess who I met at the department store today.

examples.ko: 아직 반도 안 드셨는데 그만 드시게요?
examples.en: You haven't even eaten half yet; are you stopping already?

examples.ko: 네가 좋아하는 반찬을 했는데 밥 안 먹게?
examples.en: I made the side dish you like, and you're not going to eat?

compare.difference: “-을까?” wonders; “-게?” in the quiz use asks the listener to guess and often hints that the answer is surprising.

pair.en: I wonder whom Minjun met.
Guess whom I met.

compare.difference: “-을게요” promises something the speaker will do; “-게요?” asks about the other person's intention.

pair.en: I'll stop eating now.
Are you stopping now?

pitfalls.note: In the quiz use it is “-게”, not the “-ㄹ게” of a promise.
pitfalls.en: Guess whom I met.

pitfalls.note: The informal ending needs “요” for a person you speak to politely.
pitfalls.en: Professor, are you stopping now?

label: I heard that, right?
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending for checking something one has heard: “I hear that X, is that right?, you said that…, right?”. The polite form is “-다면서요?”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-ㄴ다면서/-는다면서”, to adjective stems and past forms as “-다면서”, and to “이다” as “-라면서”. The information must come from hearsay, and the speaker asks the listener to confirm. It is spoken with rising intonation. It is informal (“반말”); the polite form adds “요”. The contraction is “-다며”.

examples.ko: 너 다음 달에 결혼 날짜 잡는다면서?
examples.en: I hear you're setting a wedding date next month, right?

examples.ko: 이번 주말에 비가 많이 온다면서요?
examples.en: I hear it will rain a lot this weekend, is that so?

examples.ko: 승규가 이번에 장학금을 받았다면서? 축하해.
examples.en: I hear Seunggyu got a scholarship this time, right? Congratulations.

examples.ko: 그 식당이 그렇게 맛있다면서요?
examples.en: I hear that restaurant is that good, is that right?

examples.ko: 내일부터 휴가라면서? 어디로 가?
examples.en: I hear your vacation starts tomorrow, right? Where are you going?

compare.difference: “-다며” is the contracted form of “-다면서”; the two mean the same.

pair.en: I hear you are leaving tomorrow, right?
I hear you are leaving tomorrow, right?

compare.difference: “-는다면서?” asks to confirm something heard from others; “-는다고?” echoes what was just said.

pair.en: I hear you are leaving tomorrow, right?
You're leaving tomorrow?

pitfalls.note: After a noun it is “-라면서”, not “-이다면서”.
pitfalls.en: I hear the exam is tomorrow, right?

label: do/is...? informal question
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending for a question. In the old “하게” style it asks a plain question, and in everyday speech it asks a question or voices a guess or a worry to oneself (“I wonder if…”). The polite form is “-나요?”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems and to adjectives (“많나?”, “바쁘나?”), and after “-었-” and “-겠-”. “이다” takes “-ㄴ가” instead (“책인가?”). The polite “-나요?” is the one most often used with a stranger or an elder. As a self-question it often goes with “어떡하나”, “있었나”. It is conversational.

examples.ko: 요즘 일이 그렇게 많나?
examples.en: Do you have that much work these days?

examples.ko: 이 길로 쭉 가면 되나요?
examples.en: Can I just keep going straight on this road?

examples.ko: 어제 무슨 일이 있었나?
examples.en: Did something happen yesterday?

examples.ko: 이제 이 일을 어떻게 하나?
examples.en: What am I going to do about this now?

examples.ko: 혹시 제가 방해가 되나요?
examples.en: Am I perhaps getting in the way?

compare.difference: “-니” is a friendly plain question to a child or a close friend; “-나요” is polite.

pair.en: Have you eaten?
Have you eaten?

compare.difference: “-나요?” asks about a fact; “-을까요?” asks for an opinion or makes a suggestion.

pair.en: Are you going now?
Shall we go now?

pitfalls.note: “이다” does not take “-나”; it takes “-ㄴ가”.
pitfalls.en: Is this a book?

label: probably so; I should have
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending with two uses: a soft guess (“it's probably so, I bet”), and a mild regret about something one did not do (“I should have, if only I had”). The polite form is “-을걸요”.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems as “-을걸”, or “-ㄹ걸” after a vowel or ㄹ (“좁을걸”, “갈걸”), to “이다” as “일걸”, and after “-었-” in the guess use. In the regret use the verb names what the speaker did not do and is often followed by “그랬다” (“더 일찍 올걸 그랬다”). It is informal; the polite form adds “요”.

examples.ko: 생각보다 집이 좁을걸.
examples.en: The house is probably smaller than you think.

examples.ko: 지금 가면 사람이 많을걸요.
examples.en: If you go now, there will probably be a lot of people.

examples.ko: 너 지금 들어가면 어머니한테 혼날걸?
examples.en: If you go in now, I bet your mother will scold you.

examples.ko: 어릴 때 더 많이 여행을 다닐걸.
examples.en: I should have traveled more when I was young.

examples.ko: 그때 사 둘걸. 지금은 값이 두 배가 됐어.
examples.en: I should have bought it back then. Now the price has doubled.

compare.difference: “-을걸” guesses at what is likely; “-는걸” reacts to a fact that is in front of you.

pair.en: It will probably snow.
Oh, it's snowing!

compare.difference: Both guess. “-을걸” simply states the guess, often lightly correcting the listener; “-을 텐데” (here sentence-final) adds the speaker's concern and hints at what should be done.

pair.en: If you go now, you'll probably be late.
If you go now, you'll probably be late, though.

pitfalls.note: To someone you speak to politely, add “요”.
pitfalls.en: Teacher, that restaurant is probably expensive.

label: I must; you should; how could I
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending with three uses: the speaker resolves or reminds themselves (“I must, I will”), the speaker tells someone what they ought to do (“you should”), and the speaker stresses that a necessary condition is lacking (“how could I, when…”).
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems as “-아야지/-어야지”, and to “이다” as “이어야지/여야지”. The polite form is “-어야지요”. In the first use it is often said to oneself. In the second the sentence may use “-었어야지” for what should have been done. In the third use the situation makes the action impossible (“시끄러워서 잠을 잘 수 있어야지”). It is informal, spoken with falling or rising intonation.

examples.ko: 이번 시험에는 꼭 붙어야지.
examples.en: I must pass this exam, no matter what.

examples.ko: 내일부터는 일찍 일어나야지.
examples.en: From tomorrow I must get up early.

examples.ko: 남에게 도움을 받았으면 너도 베풀어야지.
examples.en: If you have been helped by others, you should do kindness in return too.

examples.ko: 약속을 했으면 지켜야지.
examples.en: If you made a promise, you have to keep it.

examples.ko: 너무 시끄러워서 잠을 잘 수 있어야지.
examples.en: It's so noisy that I can't sleep at all.

compare.difference: “-어야 하다” states an obligation; “-어야지” voices a resolve or a push, often to oneself.

pair.en: I have to exercise from tomorrow.
I must exercise from tomorrow.

compare.difference: “-겠다” states a will openly; “-어야지” is often said as a resolution to oneself.

pair.en: I will exercise from tomorrow.
I must exercise from tomorrow.

pitfalls.note: To someone you speak to politely, add “요”.
pitfalls.en: Teacher, I should go first.

label: and then...? soft command
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending with two uses: asking a follow-up question that adds to what has just been said (“and…?”), and a soft instruction that leaves room for more (“first do this, and…”). The polite form is “-고요”.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems and after “-었-”, and to “이다” as “이고”. In the question use, the question goes up in tone and stands for “…and what about…?” after one has answered or been told something. In the instruction use, the sentence trails off as if a further instruction follows (“손부터 씻고”). It is informal; the polite form adds “요”.

examples.ko: 그래, 그동안 별일은 없었고?
examples.en: So, nothing much has happened in the meantime, and…?

examples.ko: 그래서 오늘 저녁에도 약속이 있고?
examples.en: And so you have plans this evening as well, and…?

examples.ko: 먼저 손부터 씻고. 그다음에 밥 먹자.
examples.en: Wash your hands first, and then we'll eat.

examples.ko: 학교는 잘 다니고 있고? 밥은 잘 먹고?
examples.en: Are you getting along at school? And are you eating well?

examples.ko: 내가 이것을 준비할 테니 너는 그것 좀 가져오고.
examples.en: I'll prepare this, so you bring that over, and…

compare.difference: “-지?” seeks confirmation; “-고?” adds a further question to what was just said.

pair.en: Nothing much happened, and…?
Nothing much happened, right?

compare.difference: A bare command is blunter; “-고” softens it and leaves room for what follows.

pair.en: You bring that over, and…
Bring that over.

pitfalls.note: To someone you speak to politely, add “요”.
pitfalls.en: Teacher, was there nothing much going on, and…?

label: you mean...?! (polite echo)
meaning_en: A sentence-final ending that echoes something just said, with surprise, disbelief or protest. This row stresses the polite forms “-다니요” and “-라니요” and the noun form “-라니”: “what do you mean, X?!”.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems as “-다니”, and after “-었-” and “-겠-”, and to “이다” as “-라니” (“-이라니”). A polite “요” is added to speak to an elder (“-다니요”, “-라니요”). It reacts to what the listener has just said, often repeating it. Verbs also take the quoted form “-ㄴ다니요/-는다니요” (“가신다니요?”). “-으라니” echoes a command. It is spoken, with rising or sharply falling intonation.

examples.ko: 벌써 가신다니요? 아직 식사도 안 하셨는데요.
examples.en: You're leaving already? You haven't even eaten yet.

examples.ko: 그 사람이 거짓말을 했다니요? 말도 안 돼요.
examples.en: That person lied, you say? That can't be.

examples.ko: 제가 선생님을 속였다니요? 그런 적 없습니다.
examples.en: That I deceived you, you say? I never did that.

examples.ko: 이게 제 책임이라니요?
examples.en: This is my responsibility, you say?

examples.ko: 저더러 그만두라니요? 이제 막 시작했는데요.
examples.en: You tell me to quit? I have only just started.

compare.difference: “-다고요?” asks the speaker to repeat or confirm; “-다니요?” protests or marvels at what was said.

pair.en: Did you say this is my responsibility?
This is my responsibility, you say?!

compare.difference: The same ending without “요” is used to someone close; “-다니요” is the polite form.

pair.en: You're leaving already?
Leaving already?

pitfalls.note: After a noun the form is “-라니요”, not “-이다니요”.
pitfalls.en: This is my responsibility, you say?

pitfalls.note: To someone you speak to politely, add “요”.
pitfalls.en: That I deceived you, you say?

label: nothing but, all I can do
meaning_en: A formal expression meaning “only, nothing but, all one can do is…”: the speaker says that there is nothing beyond the stated state or act, and it often voices modest feeling such as gratitude or surprise.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems as “-을 따름이다”, or “-ㄹ 따름이다” after a vowel or ㄹ (“감사할 따름입니다”), to “이다” as “일 따름이다”, and after “-었-”. It is used in polite or formal speech and writing, and the polite ending “-입니다” is common. It is typical of humble statements such as “I only did my duty” and of feelings.

examples.ko: 도와주셔서 그저 감사할 따름입니다.
examples.en: I am simply grateful for your help.

examples.ko: 저는 맡은 일을 묵묵히 할 따름입니다.
examples.en: I am only doing my assigned work quietly.

examples.ko: 나는 그냥 얼굴만 보러 왔을 따름이야.
examples.en: I only came to see your face.

examples.ko: 다친 사람이 없어서 다행일 따름이다.
examples.en: I am simply relieved that no one was hurt.

examples.ko: 저는 당연한 일을 했을 따름입니다.
examples.en: I only did what was natural.

compare.difference: The two are close in meaning; “-을 따름이다” is more common in humble, formal statements of feeling.

pair.en: I am simply grateful.
I am simply grateful.

compare.difference: “-을 따름이다” says that this is all there is; “-을 수밖에 없다” says there is no other choice.

pair.en: I can only be grateful.
I have no choice but to be grateful.

pitfalls.note: It takes the adnominal “-ㄹ”, not “-는”.
pitfalls.en: I am simply grateful for your help.

label: go at it, press on aggressively
meaning_en: An expression meaning to take the initiative in pressing a point, often aggressively: “to go at it, to insist on, to come right at someone by doing X”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-고 들다”, after verbs of arguing, opposing and criticizing (“따지다”, “캐다”, “우기다”, “트집을 잡다”). The subject goes at the other person or the matter, with force. With an elder the honorific is “-고 드시다”. It is not used with neutral verbs. It is common in narration and conversation.

examples.ko: 손님이 점원에게 따지고 들었다.
examples.en: The customer went at the clerk, demanding an explanation.

examples.ko: 그렇게 하나하나 캐고 들면 걸리지 않을 사람이 없다.
examples.en: If you dig into every little thing like that, there is no one who won't be caught out.

examples.ko: 작은 실수 하나에도 트집을 잡고 드는 상사 때문에 힘들다.
examples.en: I am having a hard time because of a boss who picks on every little mistake.

examples.ko: 동생이 갑자기 따지고 들어서 싸움이 났다.
examples.en: My younger sibling suddenly started arguing with me, and a fight broke out.

examples.ko: 모두가 자기 의견만 옳다고 우기고 들었다.
examples.en: Everyone insisted that only their own opinion was right.

compare.difference: “-고 있다” just says the act is going on; “-고 들다” says the subject came at it with force.

pair.en: That person is arguing.
That person went at it, arguing hard.

compare.difference: “-으려고 들다” says the subject tries to do it; “-고 들다” says the subject presses on with it.

pair.en: My younger sibling set out to argue.
My younger sibling pressed the argument.

pitfalls.note: It needs a verb of pressing or confronting, not a neutral one.
pitfalls.en: The child insisted, being unreasonable.

label: do first and see; having done, find
meaning_en: An expression with two uses: doing something first and dealing with the rest later (“do it first, then see”), and discovering something new after having done the act (“after doing X, I found…”).
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-고 보다”, and has no tense inside. In the first use it appears in “일단 -고 보자/봅시다” or “-고 본다” and shows an approach or a habit. In the second it appears as “-고 보니(까)” and is followed by a discovery or a changed state. The verb before “-고” is complete when the discovery is made. It is used in speech and writing.

examples.ko: 일단 밥부터 먹고 봅시다.
examples.en: Let's eat first and see.

examples.ko: 일단 저지르고 보는 성격이라 후회할 때도 많다.
examples.en: I tend to act first and see later, so I often regret it.

examples.ko: 차가 막혀 도착하고 보니 벌써 약속 시간이 지난 뒤였다.
examples.en: The traffic was heavy, and when I arrived I found the appointed time had already passed.

examples.ko: 음식점에서 밥을 먹고 보니 지갑이 없었다.
examples.en: After I finished eating at the restaurant, I found I had no wallet.

examples.ko: 직접 만나고 보니 생각했던 것과 전혀 다른 사람이었다.
examples.en: Once I met them in person, they were nothing like what I had thought.

compare.difference: “-어 보니” says one tried it and found; “-고 보니” says that after the act was complete one found.

pair.en: I tried it and it was good.
After I ate it, I found it wasn't mine.

compare.difference: “-다 보니” says that something came about gradually while doing; “-고 보니” says that it came out after the act was done.

pair.en: As I kept working, I got used to it.
After doing the work, I found it rewarding.

pitfalls.note: No tense goes inside it.
pitfalls.en: After I ate, I found I had no wallet.

label: partly because
meaning_en: An expression meaning that what comes before is one of several reasons for what follows: “since X and so on, I did Y”. It softens a reason by hinting that there are others.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems as “-고 해서”, to “이다” as “이고 해서”, and after “-었-”. It often follows another reason in a list (“A도 -고 B도 -고 해서”), but one reason is enough, with the sense “among other things”. The main clause states what the speaker did or decided, usually in the past or as a plan. A suggestion can follow (“시간도 늦었고 해서 이만 일어나죠”). It is conversational.

examples.ko: 모처럼 쉬는 날이고 해서 친구들과 쇼핑을 나갔다.
examples.en: It was a rare day off, among other things, so I went shopping with friends.

examples.ko: 날씨도 춥고 해서 두꺼운 옷을 입고 나왔다.
examples.en: It was cold, among other things, so I came out in thick clothes.

examples.ko: 피곤하기도 하고 날씨도 좋지 않고 해서 오늘은 외출하지 않기로 했다.
examples.en: I was tired and the weather was bad too, so I decided not to go out today.

examples.ko: 삼계탕은 영양가도 높고 맛도 있고 해서 인기가 많다.
examples.en: Samgyetang is nutritious and tasty, among other things, so it is popular.

examples.ko: 마침 근처에 왔고 해서 잠깐 들렀어요.
examples.en: I happened to be nearby, so I stopped by for a moment.

compare.difference: “-아서/어서” gives the reason; “-고 해서” softens it and hints at other reasons.

pair.en: I was tired, so I went to bed early.
I was tired among other things, so I went to bed early.

pitfalls.note: After a noun it needs “이다”: “이고 해서”.
pitfalls.wrong: 모처럼 휴일고 해서 친구들과 쇼핑을 나갔다.
pitfalls.right: 모처럼 휴일이고 해서 친구들과 쇼핑을 나갔다.
pitfalls.en: It was a rare holiday, among other things, so I went shopping with friends.

label: while at it, taking the chance
meaning_en: An expression meaning “while doing X, taking that occasion”: one does a second, related thing along with, or on the occasion of, the first.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-는 김에” for an action in progress or planned, and as “-ㄴ/은 김에” after a completed action (“간 김에”). The second action is related and is usually done by the same person, and it is often a favor or a small extra task. It is common in speech. “이왕 -ㄴ 김에” and “말이 나온 김에” are set phrases.

examples.ko: 한국어를 공부하는 김에 한국 문화도 공부하고 싶어요.
examples.en: While I'm studying Korean, I want to study Korean culture too.

examples.ko: 마트에 가는 김에 우유도 좀 사다 줘.
examples.en: Since you're going to the mart anyway, pick up some milk too.

examples.ko: 서울에 간 김에 친구도 만나고 왔다.
examples.en: Since I was in Seoul anyway, I met a friend as well.

examples.ko: 청소하는 김에 창문도 닦아야겠다.
examples.en: While I'm cleaning, I should wipe the windows too.

examples.ko: 이왕 온 김에 구경도 하고 가자.
examples.en: Since we've come anyway, let's look around before we go.

compare.difference: “-는 길에” means on the way somewhere; “-는 김에” means taking the occasion of an act.

pair.en: On the way to the mart, I bought milk.
Since I was going to the mart anyway, I bought milk.

compare.difference: “-을 겸” gives two purposes for one outing; “-는 김에” adds a second act on the occasion of the first.

pair.en: I came out partly to take a walk.
Since I was out anyway, I took a walk too.

pitfalls.note: After a completed action the form is “-ㄴ/은 김에”, not “-었는 김에”.
pitfalls.en: Since I was in Seoul, I met a friend too.

label: as is; as soon as; whenever
meaning_en: An expression with several uses: doing it just the way something is or was (“just as I do, as you saw”), immediately upon something (“as soon as”), each time something occurs (“whenever, every time”), and to the fullest (“as much as possible”).
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-는 대로”, and after a completed act as “-ㄴ/은 대로” (“본 대로”). “대로” is a bound noun that is spaced after a verb form but attached to a noun (“법대로”). “As soon as” looks to the future or a command. “될 수 있는 대로” is a set phrase meaning “as far as possible”. It is used in speech and writing.

examples.ko: 제가 발음하는 대로 따라 해 보세요.
examples.en: Please repeat just as I pronounce it.

examples.ko: 도착하는 대로 연락드리겠습니다.
examples.en: I will contact you as soon as I arrive.

examples.ko: 시간이 나는 대로 고향에 계신 부모님을 찾아뵙는다.
examples.en: Whenever I have time, I visit my parents back in my hometown.

examples.ko: 될 수 있는 대로 쉽게 설명해 주세요.
examples.en: Please explain it as simply as possible.

examples.ko: 본 대로 느낀 대로 솔직하게 말해 보세요.
examples.en: Tell it honestly, just as you saw it and felt it.

compare.difference: “-는 대로” can look ahead; “-자마자” reports what followed immediately.

pair.en: I'll call as soon as I arrive.
I called the moment I arrived.

compare.difference: Both can mean “just as”; “-는 대로” stresses doing it exactly the way something is.

pair.en: Do just as I do.
Do it as I do.

pitfalls.note: After a verb form “대로” is spaced.
pitfalls.en: Write down whatever comes to mind.

pitfalls.note: After a noun “대로” is attached.
pitfalls.en: I will handle it according to the law.

label: in the interval, while
meaning_en: An expression meaning “in the (short) interval while X goes on or X happens”: something else happens in that gap, often unnoticed.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-는 사이에” (“-는 사이” too), and after a completed act as “-ㄴ/은 사이에” (“자리를 비운 사이에”). The main clause names something that took place in that gap, and it often happens without the speaker's notice or control. It covers a short time rather than the whole duration. It is common in speech and writing.

examples.ko: 잠깐 방심하는 사이에 사고가 생길 수 있다.
examples.en: An accident can happen in a moment of carelessness.

examples.ko: 눈 깜짝하는 사이에 기회가 지나간다.
examples.en: In the blink of an eye the chance passes.

examples.ko: 내가 자리를 비운 사이에 누가 다녀갔나 보다.
examples.en: Someone seems to have come by while I was away from my seat.

examples.ko: 엄마가 시장에 간 사이에 동생이 방을 어질렀다.
examples.en: While Mom was at the market, my younger sibling made a mess of the room.

examples.ko: 모르는 사이에 시간이 훌쩍 지나갔다.
examples.en: Before I knew it, a lot of time had passed.

compare.difference: “-는 동안” covers the whole stretch of time; “-는 사이에” points to something that happens within it.

pair.en: It rained during the time I slept.
It rained while I was asleep (without my noticing).

compare.difference: The two are close in meaning; “-는 틈에” stresses an opening or chance.

pair.ko: 엄마가 안 보는 사이에 과자를 먹었다.
pair.en: I ate the snack while Mom wasn't looking.

pair.ko: 엄마가 안 보는 틈에 과자를 먹었다.
pair.en: I ate the snack in a moment when Mom wasn't looking.

pitfalls.note: It follows a verb form, not a bare noun.
pitfalls.wrong: 방심 사이에 사고가 생길 수 있다.
pitfalls.right: 방심하는 사이에 사고가 생길 수 있다.
pitfalls.en: An accident can happen in a moment of carelessness.

label: as if, as though
meaning_en: An expression meaning “as if, as though X”: what follows looks or feels like the picture the first clause gives. It is the short form of “-는 듯이”. Repeated, “-는 듯 마는 듯” means “half-heartedly, barely”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-는 듯”, to adjective stems as “-ㄴ/은 듯”, to “이다” as “인 듯”, and to a completed act as “-ㄴ/은 듯” or a future as “-ㄹ 듯”. It also joins a quoted thought (“알겠다는 듯”). It is an adverbial that describes how something is done or felt. It is different from “-는 듯하다”, which is a guess.

examples.ko: 갑자기 배가 찌르는 듯 아팠다.
examples.en: Suddenly my stomach hurt as if it were being stabbed.

examples.ko: 지수는 아무 일도 없는 듯 태연한 얼굴이었다.
examples.en: Jisu wore a calm face as though nothing were wrong.

examples.ko: 승규는 인사를 하는 듯 마는 듯 그냥 지나가 버렸다.
examples.en: Seunggyu half greeted me and just walked past.

examples.ko: 아이는 알겠다는 듯 고개를 끄덕였다.
examples.en: The child nodded as if to say they understood.

examples.ko: 하늘이 무너질 듯 천둥이 쳤다.
examples.en: Thunder rolled as if the sky would collapse.

compare.difference: “-는 듯하다” makes a guess; “-는 듯” describes what something looks or feels like.

pair.en: It looks like it will rain.
The sky is dark as if it were about to rain.

compare.difference: “-는 듯” (the bound noun “듯” after a modifier) and the ending “-듯이” (attached straight to the stem) give much the same picture.

pair.en: It hurt as if stabbed.
It hurt as if stabbed.

pitfalls.note: There is no “-었는” form; a past image uses “-ㄴ/은”.
pitfalls.en: It hurt as if I were being stabbed with a knife.

label: that, thinking that; know how to
meaning_en: An expression used with “알다” and “모르다” for a belief or its lack: “-는 줄 알았다” means “I thought that (it turned out otherwise)”, “-는 줄 몰랐다” means “I didn't realize that”, and “-ㄹ 줄 알다” means “know how to”.
