usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-는 줄”, to adjective stems as “-ㄴ/은 줄”, to “이다” as “인 줄”, to a completed act as “-ㄴ/은 줄”, and to a supposed future or an ability as “-ㄹ 줄”. “줄” is a bound noun, so it is spaced from the verb. The speaker's thought is usually mistaken or unforeseen, and for ability it is “-ㄹ 줄 알다”. It is used in speech and writing.

examples.ko: 아침마다 운동하는 게 이렇게 힘든 줄 몰랐어.
examples.en: I didn't realize that exercising every morning was this hard.

examples.ko: 책을 읽다가 날이 새는 줄도 몰랐다.
examples.en: I was reading and didn't even notice the day breaking.

examples.ko: 나는 네가 벌써 집에 간 줄 알았어.
examples.en: I thought you had already gone home.

examples.ko: 그 사람이 선생님인 줄 알고 인사를 했는데 학생이었다.
examples.en: I thought that person was a teacher and greeted them, but they were a student.

examples.ko: 너 운전할 줄 알아?
examples.en: Do you know how to drive?

compare.difference: “-는지 몰랐다” means not knowing whether or how; “-는 줄 몰랐다” means not realizing that it was so.

pair.en: I didn't know whether that person had come.
I didn't realize that person had come.

compare.difference: “-ㄹ 줄 알다” says one has the knack or know-how; “-ㄹ 수 있다” says it is possible.

pair.en: Do you know how to drive?
Can you drive?

pitfalls.note: “줄” is a bound noun, so it is spaced from the verb.
pitfalls.en: I didn't realize it was hard.

pitfalls.note: For know-how it takes “-ㄹ 줄”, not “-는 줄”.
pitfalls.en: Do you know how to drive?

label: because of, blamed on
meaning_en: An expression meaning “because of, due to X”, for a cause that leads to an undesirable result: it blames the first clause for the second.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-는 탓에”, to adjective stems as “-ㄴ/은 탓에”, to “이다” as “인 탓에”, and to a completed act as “-ㄴ/은 탓에” or “-었던 탓에”. The result is something bad or unwelcome. “-ㄴ/은 탓에” also appears with the speaker's own fault (“내가 서두른 탓에”). The opposite, a good cause, is “-는 덕분에”. It is used in speech and writing.

examples.ko: 간식을 많이 먹는 탓에 살이 계속 찐다.
examples.en: Because I eat so many snacks, I keep putting on weight.

examples.ko: 갑자기 비가 많이 오는 탓에 소풍이 연기되었다.
examples.en: Because of the sudden heavy rain, the picnic was postponed.

examples.ko: 준비가 부족했던 탓에 발표를 망쳤다.
examples.en: Because I was not prepared enough, I ruined the presentation.

examples.ko: 경기가 어려운 탓에 취업이 쉽지 않다.
examples.en: Because the economy is hard, finding a job is not easy.

examples.ko: 내가 서두른 탓에 일이 더 꼬여 버렸다.
examples.en: Because I rushed, things got more tangled.

compare.difference: “-는 덕분에” credits a good cause; “-는 탓에” blames a bad one.

pair.en: Thanks to your help, I finished.
Because you didn't help, I couldn't finish.

compare.difference: “-는 바람에” is for an incident that caused a result, usually in the past; “-는 탓에” can describe a continuing cause.

pair.en: The roads are jammed because of the rain.
It rained, so the roads got jammed.

pitfalls.note: It names a cause of something bad; a good result takes “덕분에”.
pitfalls.en: I failed because I didn't study.

label: giving examples, X or Y or the like
meaning_en: An expression for naming actions or states as examples of a kind, or for choosing one of several: “X or Y or the like, doing things such as X or Y”. It usually comes in a repeated pair.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-ㄴ다거나/-는다거나”, to adjective stems and past forms as “-다거나”, and to “이다” as “-라거나”. It is usually repeated (“A-ㄴ다거나 B-ㄴ다거나 하다”) and closed with “하다” or “하는”, giving a vague set of examples. The simple “-거나” gives plain alternatives, and the nouns of this kind take “이라든가”. It is conversational and also written.

examples.ko: 주말에는 책을 읽는다거나 영화를 본다거나 하면서 시간을 보낸다.
examples.en: On weekends I spend time doing things like reading or watching movies.

examples.ko: 기숙사에서는 음악을 크게 듣는다거나 큰 소리를 낸다거나 하면 안 된다.
examples.en: In the dormitory you must not do things such as listening to loud music or making loud noises.

examples.ko: 몸이 아프다거나 피곤하다거나 하면 무리하지 말고 쉬세요.
examples.en: If you are sick or tired or the like, don't push yourself; rest.

examples.ko: 비가 온다거나 눈이 온다거나 하는 날에는 일찍 퇴근하세요.
examples.en: On days when it rains or snows or the like, leave work early.

examples.ko: 사고가 났다거나 길이 막힌다거나 하는 일이 생기면 바로 연락 주세요.
examples.en: If something happens, such as an accident or a traffic jam, contact me right away.

compare.difference: “-거나” gives plain alternatives; “-는다거나” gives examples and is vaguer, “X or Y or the like”.

pair.en: On weekends I read or watch a movie.

pair.ko: 주말에는 책을 읽는다거나 영화를 본다거나 한다.
pair.en: On weekends I do things like reading or watching a movie.

compare.difference: “이라든가” gives noun examples; “-는다거나” gives examples of actions and states.

pair.en: I like things such as movies or exhibitions.

pair.ko: 영화를 본다거나 전시회에 간다거나 하는 것을 좋아한다.
pair.en: I like doing things such as watching movies or going to exhibitions.

pitfalls.note: After a noun the form is “-라거나”, not “-이다거나”.
pitfalls.en: People such as students or teachers came.

pitfalls.note: An adjective takes “-다거나”, with no “-는”.
pitfalls.en: If you are cold or hot or the like, please tell me.

label: I wonder if; I think maybe
meaning_en: An expression for a subjective, uncertain thought: “I wonder whether, I'm inclined to think that…”. It also expresses worry or regret over an act, as in “내가 왜 그랬나 싶다” (“why on earth did I do that?”).
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-나 싶다”, and after “-었-” and “-겠-”, and to adjectives and “이다” as “-ㄴ가 싶다” (“큰가 싶다”, “꿈인가 싶다”); after an adjective “-나 싶다” is also heard in casual speech (“너무 많나 싶다”), but “이다” always takes “-ㄴ가”. The thought is the speaker's own, hesitant or doubtful. In the second use it follows a self-question about one's own act and expresses regret or worry. “-나 싶어서” gives that thought as the reason for an act. It is used in speech and writing.

examples.ko: 같은 내용이지만 영화보다는 소설이 더 재미있지 않았나 싶다.
examples.en: The content is the same, but I think the novel may have been more interesting than the movie.

examples.ko: 아무래도 내가 선배니까 도와줘야 하지 않나 싶어서 전화를 걸었다.
examples.en: I thought that, being the senior, I probably ought to help, so I phoned.

examples.ko: 내가 왜 그랬나 싶어서 후회가 된다.
examples.en: I wonder why on earth I did that, and I regret it.

examples.ko: 이렇게 늦게까지 안 오니 무슨 일이 생겼나 싶어 걱정이 된다.
examples.en: They have not come this late, and I wonder whether something has happened, so I'm worried.

examples.ko: 혹시 내가 잘못 들었나 싶어서 다시 물어봤다.
examples.en: Wondering whether I might have heard wrong, I asked again.

compare.difference: “-나 싶다” wonders about what is or was; “-을까 싶다” wonders about what may happen, often with worry.

pair.en: I wondered whether it was raining, so I looked out the window.
I thought it might rain, so I took an umbrella.

compare.difference: The two are close in meaning; “-나 싶다” is more hesitant and more personal.

pair.en: I wonder if the novel was more interesting.
I think the novel was more interesting.

pitfalls.note: After “이다” the form is “-ㄴ가 싶다”, not “-나 싶다”.
pitfalls.en: I was so happy that I wondered whether this was a dream.

label: because of an unforeseen event
meaning_en: An expression for an unforeseen event that caused an unwelcome result: “because X happened (unexpectedly), Y came about”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-는 바람에”, and the verb before it names an event rather than a stable state (adjectives are rarely used). The main clause is a past result that is unwanted or unplanned, and it cannot be a command or a suggestion. It also takes the honorific (“가시는 바람에”). It is used in speech and writing.

examples.ko: 길이 너무 막히는 바람에 약속에 늦었어요.
examples.en: The road was so jammed that I was late for the appointment.

examples.ko: 갑자기 눈이 오는 바람에 비행기가 취소되었다.
examples.en: It suddenly snowed, so the flight was cancelled.

examples.ko: 동생이 큰 소리로 울어 대는 바람에 잠에서 깼다.
examples.en: My younger sibling kept crying loudly, so I woke up.

examples.ko: 컴퓨터가 꺼지는 바람에 작업하던 파일을 다 날렸다.
examples.en: The computer shut down, so I lost the file I was working on.

examples.ko: 휴대폰을 집에 두고 나오는 바람에 연락을 못 했다.
examples.en: I left my phone at home, so I couldn't get in touch.

compare.difference: “-아서/어서” gives any reason; “-는 바람에” stresses an unforeseen event with an unwelcome result.

pair.en: The road was jammed, so I was late.
The road got jammed, so I ended up late.

compare.difference: “-는 바람에” is for an event that caused a past result; “-는 탓에” can blame a continuing cause.

pair.en: It rained, so the roads got jammed.
The roads are jammed because of the rain.

pitfalls.note: The clause that follows cannot be a command.
pitfalls.en: The road was jammed, so I was late.

pitfalls.note: The result must be unwelcome, not a good outcome.
pitfalls.right: 밤새 공부하는 바람에 시험 시간에 졸았다.
pitfalls.en: I studied all night, so I dozed off during the exam.

label: as long as; unless
meaning_en: An expression meaning “as long as, so long as X holds”: the first clause is a premise or condition, and the main clause holds within that range. With a negative, “-지 않는 한” means “unless”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-는 한”, to adjective stems as “-ㄴ/은 한”, and to “이다” as “인 한”. “한” is a bound noun, so it is spaced from the verb (“허락하는 한”). The set phrases “내가 아는 한” (“as far as I know”) and “-지 않는 한” (“unless”) are common. The main clause states a general or continuing truth, not a single past event. It is used in speech and writing.

examples.ko: 가족이 함께 있는 한 어떤 어려움도 이겨 낼 수 있다.
examples.en: As long as the family is together, we can overcome any hardship.

examples.ko: 부모가 도와주지 않는 한 아이들이 모든 일을 스스로 하기는 어렵다.
examples.en: Unless the parents help, it is hard for children to do everything by themselves.

examples.ko: 내가 아는 한 그 사람은 거짓말을 하지 않는다.
examples.en: As far as I know, that person does not lie.

examples.ko: 건강이 허락하는 한 계속 일하고 싶다.
examples.en: I want to keep working as long as my health allows.

examples.ko: 비가 오지 않는 한 행사는 예정대로 진행됩니다.
examples.en: Unless it rains, the event will proceed as scheduled.

compare.difference: “-는 이상” rests on a settled fact; “-는 한” sets a limit or condition.

pair.ko: 내가 이 일을 맡은 이상 책임지겠다.
pair.en: Now that I've taken this job, I will take responsibility.

pair.ko: 내가 이 일을 맡는 한 책임지겠다.
pair.en: As long as I'm in charge of this job, I will take responsibility.

compare.difference: “-으면” is a plain condition; “-는 한” says that it holds only within that range.

pair.en: If it doesn't rain, I will go.
Unless it rains, I will go.

pitfalls.note: “한” is a bound noun and is spaced.
pitfalls.en: I want to work as long as my health allows.

pitfalls.note: For “unless” the verb takes “-지 않는 한”.
pitfalls.en: Unless it rains, I will go.

label: due to, caused by
meaning_en: A formal expression meaning “due to, because of X”: a noun names the cause of what follows. Before a noun it appears as “(으)로 인한” (“caused by X”).
usage: It attaches to nouns as “으로 인하여” after a final consonant, and “로 인하여” after a vowel or ㄹ (“폭설로 인하여”). The short forms are “(으)로 인해(서)”, and the modifier form is “(으)로 인한 + noun” (“지진으로 인한 피해”). It is neutral about whether the result is good or bad, and it is typical of news and reports. It does not lead into a command.

examples.ko: 지진으로 인한 사망자가 백 명이 넘는다.
examples.en: The deaths caused by the earthquake exceed one hundred.

examples.ko: 회사 사정으로 인하여 당분간 휴업합니다.
examples.en: Due to company circumstances, we will be closed for the time being.

examples.ko: 폭설로 인해 많은 항공편이 취소되었다.
examples.en: Because of the heavy snow, many flights were cancelled.

examples.ko: 과로로 인한 질병이 늘고 있다.
examples.en: Illnesses caused by overwork are increasing.

examples.ko: 잦은 비로 인해 농작물 피해가 컸다.
examples.en: Because of the frequent rain, the damage to crops was great.

compare.difference: The two are close in meaning; “(으)로 인하여” is the form for formal and written use.

pair.en: Flights were cancelled because of the heavy snow.
Flights were cancelled because of the heavy snow.

compare.difference: “(으)로 인하여” is neutral about the result; “-는 탓에” blames a bad cause.

pair.en: I succeeded thanks to my friend's help.
I failed because my friend did not help.

pitfalls.note: After a noun that ends in ㄹ the form is “로”, not “으로”.
pitfalls.en: Flights were cancelled because of the heavy snow.

label: if it were just like
meaning_en: An expression for a wistful comparison: “if only it were like X, even if just as X”. It sets one thing (a person, a time, a state) as the standard, and imagines how much better things would be if the present matched it.
usage: It attaches to nouns, especially time words and standards (“평일만 같아도”, “작년만 같아도”, “너만 같아도”). The clause that follows is a supposition that did not or does not hold, normally ending in “-을 텐데”, “-았을 텐데”, “-ㄹ 것이다”. It expresses regret, longing or a complaint. It is conversational.

examples.ko: 세상 모든 사람이 너만 같아도 살 만할 것 같아.
examples.en: If everyone in the world were just like you, I think life would be worth living.

examples.ko: 평일만 같아도 도로가 이렇게 막히지는 않을 텐데.
examples.en: If it were just a weekday, the roads wouldn't be this jammed.

examples.ko: 십 년 전만 같아도 이 정도 일은 거뜬히 했을 텐데.
examples.en: If it were ten years ago, I would have handled this much easily.

examples.ko: 지금만 같아도 더 바랄 게 없겠다.
examples.en: If it just stayed like now, there would be nothing more to wish for.

examples.ko: 작년만 같아도 이렇게 힘들지는 않았을 거야.
examples.en: If it were just like last year, it wouldn't have been this hard.

compare.difference: “만 해도” states a fact (“even as recently as X”); “만 같아도” imagines how things would be if they were like X.

pair.ko: 십 년 전만 해도 이곳은 논이었다.
pair.en: As recently as ten years ago this place was a rice paddy.

pair.ko: 십 년 전만 같아도 이곳이 이렇게 붐비지는 않을 텐데.
pair.en: If it were just like ten years ago, this place wouldn't be this crowded.

compare.difference: “-라면” is a plain condition; “만 같아도” also says the standard is a low bar.

pair.en: If it were a weekday, it wouldn't be this crowded.

pair.ko: 평일만 같아도 이렇게 붐비지 않을 텐데.
pair.en: If only it were a weekday, it wouldn't be this crowded.

pitfalls.note: The clause that follows is a supposition, usually ending in “-을 텐데”.
pitfalls.right: 평일만 같아도 도로가 이렇게 막히지는 않을 텐데.
pitfalls.en: If it were just a weekday, the roads wouldn't be this jammed.

label: keep doing, over and over
meaning_en: An expression meaning to keep doing something repeatedly or to an excessive degree, often with annoyance: “keep on, go on and on”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-아 대다/-어 대다”, usually after verbs of noise and fuss such as “떠들다”, “울다”, “웃다”, “짖다”, “졸라 대다”, “먹다”. The vowel of the stem decides “-아” or “-어”, and irregular verbs change as usual (“조르다 → 졸라 대다”). The sense is that the act is repeated or overdone; the speaker often finds it excessive. It is used in speech and writing.

examples.ko: 오랜만에 만난 우리는 신이 나게 떠들어 댔다.
examples.en: Meeting after a long time, we chattered away happily.

examples.ko: 아이가 장난감을 사 달라고 졸라 대서 결국 사 주었다.
examples.en: The child kept pestering me to buy the toy, so I finally bought it.

examples.ko: 옆집 개가 밤새 짖어 대서 한숨도 못 잤다.
examples.en: The neighbor's dog barked all night, so I did not sleep a wink.

examples.ko: 하도 웃어 대서 배가 아팠다.
examples.en: I laughed so much that my stomach hurt.

examples.ko: 아이들이 뛰어 대는 소리에 윗집에 올라갔다.
examples.en: Because of the noise of the children running around, I went up to the apartment above.

compare.difference: “-고 있다” just says an act is going on; “-어 대다” says it goes on and on, usually excessively.

pair.en: The child is crying.
The child keeps crying on and on.

compare.difference: “-곤 하다” says an act recurs from time to time; “-어 대다” says it goes on and on, to excess, often to the speaker's annoyance.

pair.en: That dog often barks at night.
That dog kept barking all night.

pitfalls.note: An irregular verb changes as usual: “조르다” becomes “졸라”.
pitfalls.wrong: 아이가 장난감을 사 달라고 조르어 댔다.
pitfalls.right: 아이가 장난감을 사 달라고 졸라 댔다.
pitfalls.en: The child kept pestering me to buy the toy.

pitfalls.note: A ㄹ-stem keeps its ㄹ before “-어”.
pitfalls.en: The children kept making noise.

label: perhaps because
meaning_en: An expression for guessing at a reason: “perhaps because X, maybe it is that X”. The speaker is not sure that the reason is the true one.
usage: It attaches to verb and adjective stems as “-아서인지/-어서인지”, and to “이다” as “이어서인지/여서인지”. Contracted forms are normal (“내려서인지”, “해서인지”). It is written as one word. The second clause states the observed result, and the guess concerns its cause. It is used in speech and writing.

examples.ko: 눈이 쌓여서인지 길이 많이 미끄러웠다.
examples.en: Perhaps because snow had piled up, the road was very slippery.

examples.ko: 어제 늦게까지 책을 읽어서인지 하루 종일 졸리다.
examples.en: Perhaps because I read late into the night yesterday, I am sleepy all day.

examples.ko: 날씨가 좋아서인지 공원에는 사람이 많았다.
examples.en: Perhaps because the weather was nice, there were many people in the park.

examples.ko: 막내여서인지 가끔 철없이 굴 때가 있다.
examples.en: Perhaps because they are the youngest, they sometimes act like a child.

examples.ko: 너무 긴장이 되어서인지 아무 말도 생각나지 않았다.
examples.en: Perhaps because I was too nervous, I could not think of anything to say.

compare.difference: “-아서/어서” states the reason as a fact; “-어서인지” guesses at it.

pair.en: It snowed, so the ground froze.
Perhaps because it snowed, the ground froze.

compare.difference: The two are close in meaning; “-는지” gives a vague reason in the same way, built on the verb or adjective itself.

pair.en: Perhaps from working hard, their face has grown thin.
Perhaps because they worked hard, their face has grown thin.

pitfalls.note: “인지” is attached to “서”, with no space.
pitfalls.wrong: 눈이 내려서 인지 바닥이 얼어 있었다.
pitfalls.en: Perhaps because it had snowed, the ground was frozen.

label: depending on; according to
meaning_en: An expression with two uses: “depending on X” (the result varies with X), and “in accordance with X” (following a rule, a plan or an instruction). The form “에 따르면” means “according to X” and introduces a source.
usage: It attaches to nouns as “에 따라(서)” and “에 따르면”, and the modifier form is “에 따른” (“계절에 따른 차이”). In the first use the main clause says that something differs or varies (“다르다”, “달라지다”). In the second it says what is done by the rule. “에 따르면” is followed by what the source says, usually in the quoting form (“-다고 한다”). The verb “따르다” in “길을 따라” (“along the road”) is a different construction.

examples.ko: 사람에 따라 좋아하는 음식이 다르다.
examples.en: Favorite foods differ depending on the person.

examples.ko: 회사의 규정에 따라 처리하겠습니다.
examples.en: I will handle it in accordance with company regulations.

examples.ko: 계절에 따라 입는 옷이 달라진다.
examples.en: The clothes one wears change depending on the season.

examples.ko: 일기예보에 따르면 내일은 비가 온다고 한다.
examples.en: According to the weather forecast, it will rain tomorrow.

examples.ko: 경찰 발표에 따르면 사고 원인은 과속이었다.
examples.en: According to the police announcement, the cause of the accident was speeding.

compare.difference: “에 따라” follows a noun; “-기에 따라” follows a verb and means “depending on how it is done”.

pair.en: The taste differs depending on the person.
The taste differs depending on how you make it.

compare.difference: “에 따르면” and “에 의하면” both mean “according to”; the two are close in meaning.

pair.en: According to the forecast, it will rain tomorrow.
According to the forecast, it will rain tomorrow.

pitfalls.note: “along a path” takes “을/를 따라”, not “에 따라”.
pitfalls.en: I walked along the road.

pitfalls.note: “에 따르면” reports a source, so the clause that follows reports it.
pitfalls.wrong: 일기예보에 따르면 저는 내일 비가 올 것 같아요.
pitfalls.right: 일기예보에 따르면 내일 비가 온다고 해요.
pitfalls.en: According to the forecast, they say it will rain tomorrow.

label: compared to
meaning_en: An expression meaning “compared to, in comparison with X”: the first noun is the standard, and what follows is the result of that comparison. “에 비하면” means “if compared to X”.
usage: It attaches to nouns as “에 비하여”, with the shortened “에 비해(서)” and the conditional “에 비하면”. The main clause states how the subject differs from the standard, such as “많이 올랐다”, “어려 보인다”, “적다”. It is not the verb “비교하다”, which takes “와/과”. It is used in speech and writing.

examples.ko: 물가가 작년에 비하여 많이 오른 것 같다.
examples.en: Prices seem to have risen a lot compared to last year.

examples.ko: 서울은 다른 도시에 비하면 교통이 편리한 편이다.
examples.en: Compared with other cities, Seoul's transport is rather convenient.

examples.ko: 지수는 나이에 비하여 훨씬 어려 보인다.
examples.en: Jisu looks much younger than their age.

examples.ko: 노력에 비하여 결과가 좋지 않았다.
examples.en: The result was poor compared to the effort.

examples.ko: 예상에 비해 참가자가 적었다.
examples.en: The number of participants was low compared to what had been expected.

compare.difference: The two are close in meaning; “에 비해” sets the first noun as a standard of comparison, and “보다” is shorter.

pair.en: Prices have risen compared with last year.
Prices are higher than last year.

compare.difference: “치고” says it is surprising for that kind of thing; “에 비해” compares with a standard.

pair.en: It is warm for winter weather.
It is warm compared with winter weather.

pitfalls.note: “비하다” takes “에”; “와/과” goes with “비교하다” (“작년과 비교해”).
pitfalls.en: Prices rose a lot compared to last year.

label: by, according to
meaning_en: A formal expression with several uses: the agent or cause of an event (“by X”), the basis or means (“by, through X”), and, as “에 의하면”, a source (“according to X”). The modifier is “에 의한”.
usage: It attaches to nouns as “에 의하여”, “에 의해(서)”, “에 의하면” and the modifier “에 의한”. After a passive verb it marks the agent (“경찰에 의해 체포되었다”), the active verb does not take it. As a basis it is followed by a decision or result (“투표에 의하여 결정되었다”), and as a source it leads into reported content. It is formal and common in news, laws and reports.

examples.ko: 범인은 경찰에 의하여 체포되었다.
examples.en: The culprit was arrested by the police.

examples.ko: 이 건물은 유명한 건축가에 의하여 설계되었다.
examples.en: This building was designed by a famous architect.

examples.ko: 조사에 의하면 청소년의 절반이 수면이 부족하다고 한다.
examples.en: According to the survey, half of teenagers do not get enough sleep.

examples.ko: 폭우에 의한 피해가 컸다.
examples.en: The damage caused by the heavy rain was great.

examples.ko: 이 문제는 투표에 의하여 결정하기로 했다.
examples.en: It was decided to settle this issue by vote.

compare.difference: “에게” marks the agent with a verb such as “잡히다”; “에 의해” marks the agent with a formal “-되다” passive.

pair.en: The thief was caught by the police.
The culprit was arrested by the police.

compare.difference: “에 의하면” and “에 따르면” both introduce a source and are close in meaning.

pair.en: According to the survey, half are short of it.
According to the survey, half are short of it.

pitfalls.note: It marks the agent of a passive verb; the active verb does not take it.
pitfalls.en: The culprit was arrested by the police.

label: finish off; end up
meaning_en: An expression meaning that an act is completely done or ended, often with relief (it is off my chest) or with regret (it can't be undone): “do away with, finish, up and do”.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-아 버리다/-어 버리다”, and the vowel of the stem decides which (“먹어 버리다”). A vowel-final stem contracts (“가 버리다”, “해 버리다”). It stresses completeness and cannot be undone, and so it often goes with things that are lost, used up or said (“다 먹어 버렸다”, “말해 버렸다”). It is common in speech and writing.

examples.ko: 지하철에서 졸다가 그만 내릴 역을 지나쳐 버렸다.
examples.en: I dozed off on the subway and ended up passing my station.

examples.ko: 배가 고파서 동생 몫까지 다 먹어 버렸다.
examples.en: I was hungry and ended up eating even my younger sibling's share.

examples.ko: 고민하던 일을 말해 버리니 속이 시원하다.
examples.en: Now that I have said what I was agonizing over, I feel relieved.

examples.ko: 승규는 피곤해서 옷을 입은 채로 잠들어 버렸다.
examples.en: Tired, Seunggyu fell asleep with clothes still on.

examples.ko: 큰 소리로 다 말해 버리고 나니 후련했다.
examples.en: After I said it all out loud, I felt relieved.

compare.difference: “-어 버리다” marks something as done and over; “-어 내다” marks something achieved by effort.

pair.en: I got all my homework done.
I saw the hard homework through to the end.

compare.difference: The two are close in meaning; both say that something is finally done or happens, often with regret.

pair.en: I ate it all up.
I ended up eating it all.

pitfalls.note: A vowel-final stem contracts with “-아/-어”.
pitfalls.en: My friend went off ahead.

label: it looks like, I gather
meaning_en: An expression for a guess drawn from a sign or circumstance: “it appears that, it looks as though”. It is about what is going on or is about to happen.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-ㄹ/을 모양이다” for what will happen, “-는 모양이다” for what is happening and “-ㄴ/은 모양이다” for what has happened, and to adjectives as “-ㄴ/은 모양이다” (“유명한 모양이다”). It needs a sign the speaker has noticed (“-는 걸 보니”). The guess is about someone or something other than the speaker. It is used in speech and writing.

examples.ko: 영수는 배탈이 난 이후로 죽만 먹더니 오늘부터는 밥을 먹을 모양이다.
examples.en: Yeongsu has eaten only porridge since the upset stomach, but it looks like they will eat rice from today.

examples.ko: 하늘이 저렇게 어두운 걸 보니 곧 비가 올 모양이다.
examples.en: The sky is that dark, so it looks like rain is coming soon.

examples.ko: 유민이가 짐을 싸는 걸 보니 내일 떠날 모양이에요.
examples.en: Yumin is packing bags, so it looks like they will leave tomorrow.

examples.ko: 사람들이 줄을 서 있는 걸 보니 그 가게가 유명한 모양이다.
examples.en: People are standing in line, so that shop seems to be famous.

examples.ko: 불이 꺼져 있는 걸 보니 모두 퇴근한 모양입니다.
examples.en: The lights are off, so it looks like everyone has left work.

compare.difference: “-을 것 같다” is a general impression; “-을 모양이다” draws on a sign that has been seen.

pair.en: I think it may rain.
It looks like rain, judging from what I see.

compare.difference: Both are guesses from what one observes; “-는 듯하다” can also soften the speaker's own opinion, which “-는 모양이다” cannot.

pair.en: It must be snowing, judging from signs.
It seems to be snowing.

pitfalls.note: An adjective takes “-ㄴ/은 모양이다”.
pitfalls.en: That shop seems to be famous.

label: nearly, almost did
meaning_en: An expression meaning that something almost happened but did not: “almost, nearly, came close to X”. It is also used to exaggerate a bad state (“I thought I would die”).
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-ㄹ/을 뻔하다”, almost always as “-ㄹ 뻔했다”. What it names did not actually happen. It is frequent with “하마터면” (“by a hair”), and with exaggerations such as “죽을 뻔했다”, “웃겨서 쓰러질 뻔했다”. It is conversational and common in narration.

examples.ko: 지수는 부모님의 사고 소식을 듣고 정신을 잃을 뻔했다.
examples.en: Hearing the news of their parents' accident, Jisu almost lost consciousness.

examples.ko: 지하철을 타지 않았으면 약속 시간에 늦을 뻔했다.
examples.en: If I hadn't taken the subway, I would have been late for the appointment.

examples.ko: 길에서 넘어질 뻔했는데 다행히 잡아 주는 사람이 있었다.
examples.en: I nearly fell on the street, but luckily someone caught me.

examples.ko: 너무 웃겨서 배꼽이 빠질 뻔했다.
examples.en: It was so funny that I nearly split my sides.

examples.ko: 아침을 못 먹었더니 배가 고파 죽을 뻔했어.
examples.en: I couldn't eat breakfast and was so hungry I thought I would die.

compare.difference: “-을 것 같다” says it seems it will happen; “-을 뻔하다” says it came close but did not.

pair.en: It seemed I would fall.
I nearly fell.

compare.difference: “-았다” says that it did happen; “-을 뻔했다” says that it nearly did.

pair.en: I fell on the street.
I nearly fell on the street.

pitfalls.note: What it names did not happen, so it cannot be followed by a result of the event.
pitfalls.en: I nearly fell, but I wasn't hurt.

pitfalls.note: It is used as a past form, “-ㄹ 뻔했다”.
pitfalls.en: I nearly fell.

label: I hear that; they say
meaning_en: A contracted expression for passing on what someone else said: “they say that, I hear that”. It is the contraction of “-는다고 해”. As a question it asks about something the listener has heard.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-ㄴ대/-는대” (“온대”, “먹는대”), to adjective stems and past forms as “-대” (“좋대”, “갔대”), and to “이다” as “-래”. A reported command is “-(으)래” and a reported suggestion is “-재”. The polite form adds “요”. The speaker did not see it, but heard it. It is used in conversation.

examples.ko: 오늘 저녁에 뷔페를 먹는대.
examples.en: I hear it's a buffet for dinner this evening.

examples.ko: 내일부터 장마가 시작된대요.
examples.en: They say the rainy season starts tomorrow.

examples.ko: 승규가 이번에 장학금을 받았대.
examples.en: I hear Seunggyu received a scholarship this time.

examples.ko: 선생님이 내일까지 숙제를 내래.
examples.en: The teacher says to hand in the homework by tomorrow.

examples.ko: 그 식당 음식이 정말 맛있대?
examples.en: Did they say the food at that restaurant is really good?

compare.difference: “-대” is what the speaker heard; “-데” is what the speaker experienced.

pair.en: I hear the food at that restaurant is good.
The food at that restaurant was good (I found).

compare.difference: “-는대” is the contraction of “-는다고 해”; the two mean the same.

pair.en: They say it will rain tomorrow.
They say it will rain tomorrow.

pitfalls.note: After a noun the form is “-래”.
pitfalls.en: I hear the exam is tomorrow.

pitfalls.note: Do not mix up “-대” (heard) with “-데” (experienced).
pitfalls.en: I hear my friend is coming tomorrow.

label: amid the chaos, because of
meaning_en: An expression meaning “because of the commotion or turmoil of X”: while a noisy, confused or pressing situation goes on, an unwelcome result follows.
usage: It attaches to verb stems as “-는 통에”, and to “없다” and “있다” as in “정신없는 통에”. The first clause names a disturbance that is in progress, and the main clause gives a bad or unintended result. It is usually past, and it cannot be followed by a command. It is spoken and written, and similar in meaning to “-는 바람에”.

examples.ko: 시험지를 빨리 내라고 재촉하는 통에 이름 쓰는 걸 잊고 말았다.
examples.en: Amid the urging to hand in the paper quickly, I forgot to write my name.

examples.ko: 아이들이 떠드는 통에 전화 소리를 못 들었다.
examples.en: With the children making noise, I couldn't hear the phone.

examples.ko: 옆집에서 공사를 하는 통에 잠을 설쳤다.
examples.en: With the construction next door, I slept badly.

examples.ko: 사람들이 한꺼번에 몰리는 통에 줄이 엉망이 되었다.
examples.en: Because people crowded in all at once, the line fell into a mess.

examples.ko: 이사하느라 정신없는 통에 중요한 서류를 잃어버렸다.
examples.en: Amid the chaos of moving, I lost an important document.

compare.difference: The two are close in meaning; “-는 통에” stresses a noisy, confused situation that is going on.

pair.ko: 아이가 우는 통에 일을 못 했다.
pair.en: With the child crying, I couldn't work.

pair.ko: 아이가 우는 바람에 일을 못 했다.
pair.en: The child cried, so I couldn't work.

compare.difference: “-는 통에” points to a turmoil in progress; “-는 탓에” blames a cause in general.

pair.en: With the construction going on, I slept badly.
Because of the construction, I slept badly.

pitfalls.note: The result must be something unwelcome.
pitfalls.right: 손님이 몰리는 통에 정신이 하나도 없었다.
pitfalls.en: With customers crowding in, I was completely frazzled.

pitfalls.note: There is no “-었는” form; the verb is in the present “-는”.
pitfalls.en: With the children making noise, I couldn't hear.
